The paradox was his sharpest weapon: he loved to utter quips that seemed self-contradictory yet struck straight to the point, puncturing the hypocrisy and earnestness of Victorian society. When everyone wore a solemn face and preached virtue, a single elegant inversion from him exposed the sham for what it was — in his hands wit was not ornament but a blade of critique.
Yet fate dealt him the cruelest irony. The three trials of 1895 cast this master of the stage into the abyss; imprisoned for a homosexual love affair, he fell from public idol to public target. In prison he wrote the long letter De Profundis, its tone wholly changed from his old lightness, gravely reflecting on suffering, humility, and the meaning of pain — the man who had defended beauty and pleasure all his life touched, at last, in the depths of jail, the true weight of tragedy. That letter, together with his comedies, fairy tales, and paradoxes, makes up the whole of Wilde: a man who resisted his age with laughter and was crushed by it.

assessments.text: 其声誉历经百年的逆转：从身败名裂的「罪人」，到被重新尊为英语文学最伟大的喜剧家与格言家之一；他的同性恋身份与受难，也使他成为现代同志平权与言论自由的文化偶像。
在权威传记《奥斯卡·王尔德》中，将其塑造为一位被时代误读、其思想之深远远超「俏皮才子」标签的人物；该书获普利策奖，对王尔德的当代经典化贡献巨大。

assessments_en.text: His reputation underwent a century-long reversal: from a disgraced "criminal" to a figure revered anew as one of the greatest comic playwrights and aphorists in the English language; his homosexuality and his suffering also made him a cultural icon of modern gay rights and free expression.

In his authoritative biography Oscar Wilde, he portrayed a man misread by his age, whose thought ran far deeper than the label of mere "witty dandy"; the book won the Pulitzer Prize and contributed greatly to Wilde's modern canonization.

quotes: 我们都身处沟渠之中，但仍有人仰望星空。（《温德米尔夫人的扇子》）
我能抵抗一切，除了诱惑。（《温德米尔夫人的扇子》）
生活模仿艺术，远甚于艺术模仿生活。（《谎言的衰朽》）
世上没有道德或不道德的书，书只有写得好与写得坏之分。（《道林·格雷的画像》序）
quotes_en: We are all in the gutter, but some of us are looking at the stars. (Lady Windermere's Fan)
I can resist everything except temptation. (Lady Windermere's Fan)
Life imitates Art far more than Art imitates Life. (The Decay of Lying)
There is no such thing as a moral or an immoral book. Books are well written, or badly written. (Preface to The Picture of Dorian Gray)
wilde.lineage: 师承沃尔特·佩特与约翰·罗斯金所代表的唯美主义与艺术哲学，上溯法国的戈蒂耶「为艺术而艺术」之说；其唯美姿态、悖论文风与喜剧技艺，深刻影响了现代戏剧、格言文学与同志文化，至今仍是引用率最高的英语作家之一。
wilde.lineage_en: Schooled in the Aestheticism and art-philosophy of Walter Pater and John Ruskin, and reaching back to Gautier's French doctrine of "art for art's sake," his aesthetic pose, paradoxical style, and comic craft deeply influenced modern drama, the literature of the aphorism, and gay culture, and he remains one of the most-quoted writers in English.
wilde.trivia: 据传他在纽约海关报关时妙语：「除了我的天才，我没有什么要申报的。」临终困居巴黎一家寒酸旅馆，又留下名言：「我和这墙纸正在进行一场殊死决斗，不是它死，就是我亡。」最终他先走一步。他以皈依天主教告别人世。
wilde.trivia_en: He is said to have quipped at New York customs, "I have nothing to declare except my genius." Dying in a shabby Paris hotel, he reportedly said, "My wallpaper and I are fighting a duel to the death. One or the other of us has to go." In the end he went first. He was received into the Catholic Church on his deathbed.

nussbaum.bio: 1947– ，美国哲学家，芝加哥大学法学与伦理学教授，著述横跨古希腊伦理、政治哲学、女性主义与情感理论，是当代最具影响力的公共哲学家之一。
nussbaum.bio_en: 1947– , an American philosopher, professor of law and ethics at the University of Chicago, writing across ancient Greek ethics, political philosophy, feminism, and the theory of emotions — one of the most influential public philosophers alive.
nussbaum.ideas:
努斯鲍姆最有名的，是和经济学家阿马蒂亚·森一起发展的「能力进路」。它问的是一个朴素却尖锐的问题：衡量一个社会好不好，不该只看 GDP 或人均收入，而要看——**人们实际上能够去『做』什么、能够『成为』什么样的人**。一个国家再富，如果女性不能自由出门、穷人没机会受教育，那这些财富对他们就是空的。
她进一步列了一张「核心能力」清单（约十项），当作有尊严的人生的底线：活到正常寿命、身体健康与不受暴力、能运用感官与想象去思考、能有情感依恋、能做实践理性的选择、能与他人平等交往、能玩、能对自己的环境有一定掌控……一个正派的社会，有义务把每个人都托到这条线以上。
她还为「情感」翻案。主流哲学常把情感当成理性的敌人；她在《思想的剧变》里论证：恐惧、悲伤、爱、同情其实都包含判断——它们是我们认定『什么重要』的方式，因此是伦理生活的核心，而非干扰。
由此她特别看重文学与人文教育：读小说、进入别人的处境，能训练一种「叙事想象力」与同理心，而这正是民主社会不可或缺的能力。她的整套思想，是一种接续亚里士多德的、关于『人如何才能繁盛』的现代伦理学，并一路通向女性主义与全球正义。
nussbaum.ideas_en:
Nussbaum is best known for the “capabilities approach,” which she developed with the economist Amartya Sen. It asks a plain but pointed question: to judge how well a society is doing, don’t look only at GDP or average income — look at what people are actually **able to do and able to be**. However rich a country is, if women can’t leave the house freely or the poor have no shot at education, that wealth is empty for them.
She goes further and lists about ten “central capabilities” as a floor for a life of dignity: to live a normal lifespan; bodily health and freedom from violence; to use the senses and imagination to think; to form emotional attachments; to exercise practical reason; to associate with others as an equal; to play; to have some control over one’s environment. A decent society, she argues, is obliged to lift everyone above that line.
She also rehabilitates the emotions. Mainstream philosophy often treats them as reason’s enemy; in Upheavals of Thought she argues that fear, grief, love, and compassion all contain judgments — they are how we register what matters, and so are central to the ethical life, not a distraction from it.
Hence her stress on literature and a humanities education: reading novels and entering others’ situations trains a “narrative imagination” and empathy that a democracy cannot do without. The whole project is a modern, neo-Aristotelian ethics of human flourishing that runs onward into feminism and global justice.

assessments.text: 诺奖经济学家、能力进路的共同开创者，与其长期合作，将这一框架引入联合国的『人类发展』衡量体系。
被广泛视为当代最重要的公共哲学家之一；也有批评者认为她的『核心能力清单』带有特定文化预设、难称中立。

assessments_en.text: The Nobel-winning economist and co-founder of the capabilities approach, her long-time collaborator; the framework shaped the UN’s Human Development measures.
Widely regarded as one of the most important living public philosophers; critics argue her list of “central capabilities” carries particular cultural assumptions and is not truly neutral.

quotes: 衡量一个国家，要看它最弱势的成员过得怎样。（大意）
同情，是把另一个人的苦难，当作与自己相关的事。（大意）
quotes_en: The measure of a nation is how its most vulnerable members fare. (paraphrased)
Compassion is taking another person’s suffering as something that concerns oneself. (paraphrased)
works: 《告别功利：为何民主需要人文学科》
works_en: Upheavals of Thought: The Intelligence of Emotions
Not for Profit: Why Democracy Needs the Humanities
nussbaum.lineage: 承亚里士多德的德性伦理与古希腊悲剧；与阿马蒂亚·森共建能力进路；影响发展经济学、人权理论、动物伦理与女性主义政治哲学。
nussbaum.lineage_en: Draws on Aristotelian virtue ethics and Greek tragedy; co-built the capabilities approach with Amartya Sen; influences development economics, human-rights theory, animal ethics, and feminist political philosophy.
nussbaum.trivia: 她以惊人的多产著称（数十部著作横跨多个领域）；也以为非人动物的『能力』与权利辩护、把同理心训练放进民主教育而广受讨论。
nussbaum.trivia_en: Famously prolific (dozens of books across many fields); also widely discussed for extending the capabilities argument to the rights of non-human animals and for putting the training of empathy at the heart of democratic education.

mengzi.bio: 孟子（约前372–前289），名轲，战国时期邹国人，是继孔子之后儒家最重要的思想家，后世尊为『亚圣』。他相传受业于孔子之孙子思的门人，一生周游列国，游说齐宣王、梁惠王等君主推行『仁政』，却大多不被采纳，晚年退而与弟子著书，成《孟子》七篇。他的思想以性善论为核心，气象雄辩、锋芒毕露，对后世儒学尤其是宋明理学影响极深。
mengzi.bio_en: Mengzi (Mencius, c. 372–289 BC), personal name Ke, was a native of the state of Zou in the Warring States period and the most important Confucian thinker after Confucius himself, revered by later ages as the 'Second Sage.' He is said to have studied under the school of Zisi, Confucius's grandson. He travelled among the feudal states, urging rulers such as King Xuan of Qi and King Hui of Liang to adopt 'benevolent government,' but was mostly ignored; in old age he withdrew to compose, with his disciples, the seven books of the Mengzi. His thought centres on the innate goodness of human nature; eloquent and combative in style, it shaped later Confucianism — especially the Neo-Confucianism of the Song and Ming — profoundly.
mengzi.ideas:
孟子思想的地基是『性善论』：人性本来是善的。他不是说人天生就是圣人，而是说人生来就带着善的『萌芽』——他称之为『四端』：恻隐之心（不忍别人受苦）、羞恶之心（对可耻之事的排斥）、辞让之心（谦让）、是非之心（分辨对错），分别是仁、义、礼、智四种德性的开端。

他用一个著名的思想实验来证明：任何人突然看见一个孩子快要掉进井里，都会心头一紧、生出救护之念——这一瞬间的不忍，不为讨好孩子父母，也不为博取名声，纯是本心的自然流露。既然人人都有这颗『不忍人之心』，善就不是外面强加的，而是本自具足、只待培养。

于是修养的关键在『扩充』：把这点微弱的萌芽像浇灌禾苗一样养大，而不是从外面塞进一套规矩。他也把这套人性论推到政治上，主张『仁政』『王道』——君主若能推己及人、保民而王，天下自然归心；并喊出振聋发聩的『民为贵，社稷次之，君为轻』。他还讲『浩然之气』：一种由内在道义长期积累、充塞天地的正大之气，让人『富贵不能淫，贫贱不能移，威武不能屈』。
mengzi.ideas_en:
The foundation of Mengzi's thought is the doctrine that human nature is good. He did not mean that people are born sages, but that they come into the world already bearing the 'sprouts' of goodness — what he called the 'four sprouts': the heart of compassion (the inability to bear another's suffering), the heart of shame, the heart of deference, and the heart that tells right from wrong — the beginnings, respectively, of benevolence, righteousness, ritual propriety and wisdom.

He argued this with a famous thought experiment: anyone who suddenly saw a child about to fall into a well would feel a jolt of alarm and the impulse to save it — an impulse aimed neither at winning the parents' favour nor at earning a good name, but flowing naturally from the original heart. Since everyone has this 'heart that cannot bear the suffering of others,' goodness is not imposed from outside but already present, waiting only to be cultivated.

The key to self-cultivation, then, is 'extension' (kuochong): to nourish these faint sprouts as one waters a seedling, rather than to cram in a code of rules from without. He carried this view of human nature into politics, advocating 'benevolent government' and the 'kingly way' — a ruler who extends his own feeling to his people will win the realm's heart — and issued the ringing declaration that 'the people are the most precious, the altars of state next, the ruler the lightest.' He also spoke of the 'flood-like qi,' a vast and upright vital energy, accumulated through long inner rightness, that lets a person be 'incorruptible by riches, unmoved by poverty, unbent by force.'

assessments.text: 将《孟子》列入『四书』，与《论语》《大学》《中庸》并尊，视孟子为孔门心法的正传，奠定其后世经典地位。
在《原道》中构建儒家『道统』，称孔子之后其道独传于孟子，孟死则道不得其传，极力推尊。

assessments_en.text: Placed the Mengzi among the 'Four Books' alongside the Analects, the Great Learning and the Doctrine of the Mean, treating Mengzi as the true transmitter of the Confucian teaching of the heart and fixing his canonical status.

In his 'Essentials of the Moral Way' constructed a Confucian 'orthodox lineage,' holding that after Confucius the Way passed to Mengzi alone, and that with his death its transmission was broken — an emphatic elevation.

quotes: 恻隐之心，人皆有之。
富贵不能淫，贫贱不能移，威武不能屈，此之谓大丈夫。
民为贵，社稷次之，君为轻。
quotes_en: The heart of compassion is possessed by all people.
Riches cannot corrupt him, poverty cannot shift him, force cannot bend him — this is what it means to be a great man.
The people are the most precious, the altars of state come next, and the ruler is the lightest.
works: 《孟子》（七篇，如《梁惠王》《公孙丑》《告子》《尽心》）
works_en: The Mengzi (Mencius), in seven books — including 'King Hui of Liang,' 'Gongsun Chou,' 'Gaozi' and 'Exhausting the Heart'
mengzi.lineage: 上承孔子，经孔子之孙子思一系（『思孟学派』）而下传，与主张性恶的荀子并为儒家两大源流。其性善说经唐代韩愈表彰、宋代朱熹列入四书而成官学正统，深塑宋明理学乃至东亚儒家教育。
mengzi.lineage_en: He inherited from Confucius through the line of Zisi, Confucius's grandson (the 'Zisi–Mengzi school'), and together with Xunzi, who held that nature is bad, formed the two great wellsprings of Confucianism. His doctrine of innate goodness, championed by Han Yu in the Tang and canonised by Zhu Xi among the Four Books in the Song, became state orthodoxy and deeply shaped Neo-Confucianism and East Asian Confucian education.
mengzi.trivia: 『孟母三迁』的故事流传千古：相传孟母为给幼子择良好环境，三次搬家——避开墓地、市集，最终定居学宫之旁；又有『断机教子』，以割断织到一半的布，警示中途辍学之害。这些故事真伪难考，却成为中国『家教』与母教的经典象征。
mengzi.trivia_en: The tale of 'Mother Meng's three moves' has been told for millennia: to secure a good environment for her young son, she is said to have moved house three times — away from a graveyard, away from a market, and finally to settle beside a school; and in 'cutting the loom to teach her son,' she severed a half-woven cloth to warn against abandoning study midway. However uncertain their historicity, these stories became classic emblems of parental instruction and the influence of mothers in China.

xunzi.bio: 荀子（约前313–前238），名况，战国末期赵国人，儒家集大成的思想家。他曾三度出任齐国稷下学宫的『祭酒』（学界领袖），后游历秦、赵，晚年任楚国兰陵令并终老于此。他博采诸家、长于论辩，学生中出了韩非与李斯两位法家与秦制的关键人物。传世《荀子》三十二篇，说理严密、气象宏阔，是先秦思想的一座高峰，却因主张『性恶』而在后世正统儒学中长期受冷落。
xunzi.bio_en: Xunzi (c. 313–238 BC), personal name Kuang, was a native of the state of Zhao at the close of the Warring States period and the great synthesiser of Confucian thought. He served three times as 'libationer' — the presiding elder — of the Jixia Academy in Qi, later travelled to Qin and Zhao, and in old age became magistrate of Lanling in Chu, where he died. Wide-ranging and formidable in argument, he numbered among his students Han Fei and Li Si, the key figures of Legalism and the Qin system. The surviving Xunzi, in thirty-two essays, is rigorous and expansive — a peak of pre-Qin thought — yet its doctrine that human nature is bad left it long neglected within later Confucian orthodoxy.
xunzi.ideas:
荀子最著名的命题是『人之性恶，其善者伪也』。这里的『伪』不是虚伪，而是『人为』——人后天有意识的努力与建构。他说人生来只有饥而欲食、劳而欲息的自然欲望，若放任不管，争夺混乱必然而生；善不是天生的，而是靠礼义教化、师法约束一点点『做』出来的。

所以他提出『化性起伪』：像用檃栝（矫正木材的工具）把弯木压直、用砺石把钝金磨利一样，人要靠外在的礼、法、师长把粗糙的天性一步步改造成德性。这条路的关键词是『积』——『积善成德』，德性是长期积累的结果，不是灵光一现。他因此极重教育与环境，《劝学》开篇『学不可以已』『青，取之于蓝而青于蓝』正是此意。

他还有一层常被忽视的深刻：『天人之分』。他主张『天行有常，不为尧存，不为桀亡』——自然有它自己的规律，不因人的善恶而赏罚；与其迷信祈求上天，不如『制天命而用之』，认识规律、加以利用。这是一种清醒的、近乎自然主义的态度，把道德的责任完全交还给人自己。
xunzi.ideas_en:
Xunzi's most famous thesis is that 'human nature is bad; its goodness is a matter of deliberate effort.' The word here rendered 'deliberate effort' (wei) does not mean falsehood but 'the man-made' — conscious, acquired striving and construction. People, he said, are born with nothing but natural appetites — to eat when hungry, to rest when tired; left unchecked, these breed strife and disorder. Goodness is not innate but something 'made,' bit by bit, through the teaching of ritual and the discipline of teachers and law.

Hence his programme of 'transforming nature and raising up deliberate effort': just as one uses a press to straighten warped wood and a whetstone to sharpen dull metal, a person must be reshaped, step by step, from crude nature into virtue by external ritual, law and instruction. The key word on this road is 'accumulation' — 'accumulate good and it becomes virtue'; character is the fruit of long build-up, not a sudden flash. He therefore prized education and environment: the opening of his 'Exhortation to Learning' — 'learning must never cease,' 'indigo is drawn from the indigo plant, yet is bluer than the plant' — carries just this meaning.

He held a further, often overlooked depth: the 'division between Heaven and man.' 'Heaven's course is constant,' he wrote; 'it does not survive for a sage-king nor perish for a tyrant.' Nature has its own regularities and does not reward or punish according to human virtue; rather than superstitiously praying to Heaven, one should 'master the mandate of Heaven and use it' — understand its laws and put them to work. This is a clear-eyed, nearly naturalistic stance that hands the whole responsibility for morality back to human beings themselves.

assessments.text: 在《仁学》中断言『二千年来之学，荀学也，皆乡愿也』，把两千年的专制学术根源上溯到荀子——虽是批评，却反证其影响之巨。
作《荀卿论》，批评荀子言辞激切，遂启李斯焚书之祸，代表后世正统对其『性恶』与法家流弊的疑虑。

assessments_en.text: In his 'Study of Benevolence' declared that 'the learning of the past two thousand years is the learning of Xunzi, and all of it is that of the village worthy' — tracing the roots of autocratic scholarship back to Xunzi; a criticism, yet one that testifies to his enormous influence.

In his 'Essay on Xunzi' faulted him for fierce, extreme rhetoric that opened the way to Li Si's burning of the books — representing the doubts of later orthodoxy about his 'bad nature' thesis and its Legalist afterlife.

quotes: 人之性恶，其善者伪也。
锲而舍之，朽木不折；锲而不舍，金石可镂。
天行有常，不为尧存，不为桀亡。
quotes_en: Human nature is bad; its goodness is a matter of deliberate effort.
Carve and give up, and rotten wood will not break; carve without ceasing, and metal and stone can be engraved.
Heaven's course is constant: it does not survive for the sage-king Yao, nor perish for the tyrant Jie.
works: 《荀子》（三十二篇，含《劝学》《性恶》《天论》《正名》《礼论》等）
works_en: The Xunzi (thirty-two essays, including 'Exhortation to Learning,' 'Human Nature is Bad,' 'Discourse on Heaven,' 'Rectifying Names' and 'Discourse on Ritual')
xunzi.lineage: 与孟子同出儒门而立异：孟主性善、荀主性恶，构成儒家人性论的两极。他集先秦诸子之长，融礼入法；弟子韩非、李斯将其思想推向法家与秦朝集权，也因此使他在后世正统儒学中长期被边缘化，直到近代才被重新重视。
xunzi.lineage_en: He came from the same Confucian school as Mengzi but took the opposite line: where Mengzi held nature good, Xunzi held it bad, and together they form the two poles of the Confucian theory of human nature. He gathered the strengths of the pre-Qin masters and folded ritual into law; his students Han Fei and Li Si pushed his thought toward Legalism and Qin centralisation, which also left him long marginalised within later Confucian orthodoxy, until he was reappraised in modern times.
xunzi.trivia: 他门下出了韩非与李斯——两位把秦国推向法家集权的关键人物，一个成为法家集大成的理论家，一个成为焚书坑儒的秦相；一位主张『化性起伪』、极重礼教的儒者，却教出了掀翻儒学的弟子，成为思想史上耐人寻味的反差。
xunzi.trivia_en: From his school came Han Fei and Li Si — the two figures who drove Qin toward Legalist centralisation, one becoming the great theorist of Legalism, the other the Qin chancellor behind the burning of books and burying of scholars. That a Confucian who preached 'transforming nature through effort' and prized ritual instruction should have trained the very pupils who overturned Confucianism is one of the intriguing ironies of intellectual history.

laozi.bio: 约前6世纪—前5世纪(生卒年不详,生平多传说),相传姓李名耳,字聃,春秋时期人,曾任周朝管理典籍的「守藏室之史」(类似国家图书馆馆长)。道家学派的奠基者,相传留下五千言的《道德经》(又名《老子》),成为道家与后世道教的根本经典,对中国乃至东亚的哲学、艺术、政治影响极其深远。
laozi.bio_en: c. 6th–5th century BC (exact dates unknown, his life largely the stuff of legend), traditionally said to be surnamed Li, named Er, styled Dan, a man of the Spring and Autumn period who served as the Zhou court's "keeper of the archives" (something like a national librarian). He is the founder of Daoism, credited with leaving behind the roughly five-thousand-character Dao De Jing (also called the Laozi), the root classic of Daoist philosophy and the later Daoist religion, and a work of immense influence on the philosophy, art, and politics of China and East Asia.
laozi.ideas:
老子思想的核心,是一个看似玄妙、其实极深的字:「道」。《道德经》开篇就说「道可道,非常道」——能用语言说清楚的「道」,就已经不是那个真正的、永恒的「道」了。这听起来像绕口令,但意思很实在:「道」是宇宙万物的总根源和总规律,它先于天地、生养万物,却又无形无声、无法被命名和定义。我们的语言和概念都太有限,一旦试图框住它,就把它给框死了。所以老子说「道」,更像是在用手指月——你要顺着手指去看月亮,而不是死盯着手指。
那这个「道」要我们怎么活?老子给的关键词是「自然」和「无为」。这两个词最容易被误解。「自然」不是指大自然山水,而是「自己如此」「本来的样子」——让万物按它自身的节奏和天性去生长,不去横加干涉。「无为」更不是「什么都不做、躺平摆烂」,而是「不妄为」——不违背事物本性地强行去作为。他打了个绝妙的比方:最好的统治、最好的处世,要像水一样。「上善若水」:水滋养万物却从不与万物相争,总是流向人人都嫌弃的低洼之处,看似柔弱,却能穿石、能载舟、能容纳百川。这就是「以柔克刚」「柔弱胜刚强」的智慧——天下最柔软的东西,反而能驾驭最坚硬的东西。
老子还有一套深刻的辩证思维,看穿了对立面的相互依存和转化。他说「有无相生,难易相成」,「祸兮福之所倚,福兮祸之所伏」——灾祸里藏着福气的转机,福气里也潜伏着灾祸的种子,好与坏从来不是绝对的,会在一定条件下互相转化。所以真正的智者懂得「物极必反」:任何事情推到极端,就会走向它的反面。强硬到顶点便趋于折断,柔弱守下反能长久。这种「不争」「守柔」「知足」的态度,不是消极怯懦,而是一种看透了规律之后的高明——「夫唯不争,故天下莫能与之争」,正因为我不争,所以天下没有谁能争得过我。
落到政治上,老子主张「无为而治」:最高明的统治者,是让百姓几乎感觉不到他的存在,不折腾、不扰民,让社会按自身规律平稳运转,「治大国若烹小鲜」——治理大国就像煎小鱼,不能老去翻动它,否则就翻烂了。他甚至描绘了一个「小国寡民」的理想:社会回归简朴,人们安居乐业,不被无尽的欲望和繁复的制度所累。
老子的智慧,本质上是教人「放下」与「顺应」:放下过度的控制欲、占有欲和争强好胜,顺应事物本来的规律。在这个人人焦虑内卷、拼命想抓住更多的时代,这份「无为」「不争」「守柔」「知足」的古老东方智慧,反而像一剂清凉的解药,至今被全世界无数人反复品读。
laozi.ideas_en:
At the heart of Laozi's thought is one word, seemingly mystical yet profoundly deep: the "Dao" (the Way). The Dao De Jing opens by saying, "The Dao that can be spoken is not the eternal Dao"—any "Way" that can be pinned down in words is already not the true, everlasting Way. This sounds like a riddle, but its point is concrete: the Dao is the ultimate source and governing pattern of all things, prior to heaven and earth, giving birth to and nourishing everything, yet itself formless, soundless, beyond naming or defining. Our language and concepts are too limited; the moment we try to box it in, we kill it. So when Laozi speaks of the Dao it is like pointing at the moon—you should follow the finger to see the moon, not fix your stare on the finger.
So how does the Dao tell us to live? Laozi's keywords are "ziran" (the natural, the self-so) and "wuwei" (non-action). Both are easily misread. "Ziran" does not mean nature's landscapes but "so of itself," "the way things already are"—letting all things grow at their own rhythm and according to their own nature, without forced interference. "Wuwei" certainly does not mean "do nothing, lie flat and rot," but "do not act recklessly"—not forcing action against the nature of things. He offers a marvelous image: the best governing, the best way of moving through the world, should be like water. "The highest good is like water": water nourishes all things yet never contends with them, always flowing to the low places everyone disdains; seemingly weak, it can wear through stone, carry boats, and gather a hundred rivers. This is the wisdom of "the soft overcoming the hard": the softest thing in the world can master the hardest.
Laozi also held a deep dialectical insight into how opposites depend on and turn into one another. "Being and non-being give birth to each other; difficult and easy complete each other," and "disaster is what fortune leans on; fortune is where disaster hides"—within calamity lies the turning point toward blessing, and within blessing lurks the seed of calamity; good and bad are never absolute and will, under the right conditions, transform into each other. So the truly wise understand that "when a thing reaches its extreme it reverses": push anything to its limit and it turns into its opposite. Pushed to the peak of hardness, a thing tends to snap; keeping to softness and the low, it endures. This stance of "not contending," "keeping to the soft," and "knowing contentment" is not passive cowardice but a higher cleverness born of seeing through the patterns—"precisely because I do not contend, no one under heaven can contend with me."
Applied to politics, Laozi advocated "governing through non-action": the finest ruler is one whose presence the people barely feel, who does not meddle or harass them, letting society run smoothly by its own laws—"governing a great state is like cooking a small fish," which you must not keep poking and turning, or it falls apart. He even sketched an ideal of "a small state with few people": society returning to simplicity, people living and working in peace, unburdened by endless desire and elaborate institutions.
Laozi's wisdom, at its core, teaches us to "let go" and "go along with": to release the excess urge to control, to possess, to compete and dominate, and to flow with the inherent patterns of things. In an age where everyone is anxious, caught in relentless competition, scrambling to grasp ever more, this ancient Eastern wisdom of non-action, non-contention, softness, and contentment reads instead like a cooling antidote—still pored over by countless people around the world today.

assessments.text: 《史记·老子韩非列传》记孔子曾问礼于老子,出而赞叹老子「其犹龙邪」——如龙一般,乘风云而上天,不可捉摸。
《庄子·天下》篇推尊老聃为「古之博大真人」,以「关尹、老聃乎,古之博大真人哉」称许其学说之宏阔。

assessments_en.text: The Records of the Grand Historian recounts that Confucius once asked Laozi about ritual and, on leaving, exclaimed that Laozi "is like a dragon"—riding the wind and clouds up into the heavens, beyond all grasping.
The "All Under Heaven" chapter of the Zhuangzi honors Lao Dan as "a vast and true man of antiquity," praising the breadth and grandeur of his teaching.

quotes: 道可道,非常道;名可名,非常名。(《道德经》第一章)
上善若水。水善利万物而不争。(《道德经》第八章)
quotes_en: The Dao that can be spoken is not the eternal Dao; the name that can be named is not the eternal name. (Dao De Jing, ch. 1)
The highest good is like water. Water benefits all things yet does not contend. (Dao De Jing, ch. 8)
works: 《道德经》(又名《老子》,分《道经》《德经》,共约五千言)
works_en: Dao De Jing (also called the Laozi, divided into the "Classic of the Way" and the "Classic of Virtue," about five thousand characters in all)
laozi.lineage: 道家开山祖师,下启庄子,合称「老庄」,形成与儒家分庭抗礼的中国思想另一大主流;汉初「黄老之学」以其「无为」治国;后世被道教尊为「太上老君」;并深刻影响中国的艺术、养生与禅宗,二十世纪起广受西方关注。
laozi.lineage_en: The founding patriarch of Daoism, he was followed by Zhuangzi (the two together called "Lao-Zhuang"), forming the other great mainstream of Chinese thought standing opposite Confucianism. Early Han "Huang-Lao" statecraft governed by his "non-action"; later Daoist religion venerated him as the "Supreme Lord Lao." He deeply shaped Chinese art, longevity practices, and Chan Buddhism, and has drawn wide Western attention since the twentieth century.
laozi.trivia: 相传老子见周室衰微,便骑着青牛西出函谷关归隐。守关的官员关尹见紫气东来,知有圣人将至,恳请他著书留言,老子遂写下五千言的《道德经》,随后飘然出关,从此不知所终——这「紫气东来」「骑青牛出关」遂成千古佳话。
laozi.trivia_en: Legend tells that, seeing the Zhou dynasty in decline, Laozi rode a black ox westward through the Hangu Pass to withdraw from the world. The pass's keeper, Yin Xi, saw a purple haze drifting in from the east and knew a sage was coming; he begged Laozi to leave behind his teaching, whereupon Laozi wrote the five thousand characters of the Dao De Jing and then passed beyond the frontier, never to be heard of again—giving rise to the timeless phrases "the purple haze comes from the east" and "riding the black ox out through the pass."

huineng.bio: 慧能（638–713），中国禅宗第六祖，被尊为南宗禅的开创者。相传他出身岭南、家贫失学、以砍柴为生，一次听人诵《金刚经》至『应无所住而生其心』而有所悟，遂北上投五祖弘忍门下。他在碓房舂米八月，因一首偈子得弘忍暗授衣钵，成为六祖，却为避争端南遁隐居多年，后于曹溪弘法。其弟子记录的《六祖坛经》是唯一一部被中国人尊称为『经』的本土佛教著作，影响遍及东亚。
huineng.bio_en: Huineng (638–713) was the Sixth Patriarch of Chinese Chan (Zen) Buddhism, revered as the founder of the Southern school. He is said to have come from Lingnan in the far south, too poor to be schooled, earning his living gathering firewood; hearing someone recite the Diamond Sutra — 'let the mind arise while dwelling on nothing' — he was awakened and travelled north to the Fifth Patriarch, Hongren. He pounded rice in the threshing shed for eight months, and on the strength of a single verse received from Hongren the secret transmission of the robe and bowl, becoming the Sixth Patriarch; then, to avoid strife, he went into hiding in the south for years before teaching openly at Caoxi. The Platform Sutra recorded by his disciples is the only native Chinese Buddhist text honoured with the title 'sutra,' and its influence spread across East Asia.
huineng.ideas:
慧能的禅法核心是『顿悟』——觉悟不必经年累月、层层修证，而可以在一念之间当下直了。这背后是他对人性的根本看法：『自性本自清净』，人人本来就具足佛性，只因妄念遮蔽而不自知。所以成佛不是从外面得到什么、修出一个新的自己，而是『明心见性』——拨开妄念，认出本来就在那里的真性。

最能代表他的是那则偈子的公案。神秀主张『身是菩提树，心如明镜台，时时勤拂拭，勿使惹尘埃』——把修行比作不断擦拭、渐渐清净；慧能却答『菩提本无树，明镜亦非台，本来无一物，何处惹尘埃』——连那面要擦的镜子、要拂的尘都本来空无，何须一点点擦？这就是『渐修』与『顿悟』的分野。

他因此讲『无念、无相、无住』：不是什么都不想，而是念起而不被念缚、不执着、不停驻。他还主张『定慧一体』（禅定与智慧本是一回事）、『烦恼即菩提』（烦恼与觉悟并非两物），以及『不立文字』——真谛不在经卷文句里，而要在自心亲证。这种直指人心、贴近日常的风格，让禅宗在中国真正落地生根。
huineng.ideas_en:
The heart of Huineng's Chan is 'sudden awakening' — enlightenment need not come through years of graded, layered practice but can break through directly in a single thought. Behind this lies his root view of human nature: 'one's own nature is originally pure'; everyone already possesses the Buddha-nature in full, and fails to know it only because deluded thoughts obscure it. To become a Buddha, then, is not to acquire something from outside or cultivate a new self, but to 'see one's true nature' — to part the deluded thoughts and recognise the real nature that was there all along.

He is best captured by the koan of the competing verses. Shenxiu proposed: 'The body is the bodhi-tree, the mind a bright mirror-stand; time and again wipe it clean, and let no dust alight' — likening practice to ceaseless polishing toward gradual purity. Huineng answered: 'Bodhi is originally no tree, nor is the bright mirror a stand; from the first not one thing exists — where could the dust alight?' — if even the mirror to be wiped and the dust to be brushed are originally empty, what is there to polish bit by bit? This is the very divide between 'gradual cultivation' and 'sudden awakening.'

Hence he taught 'no-thought, no-form, no-abiding' — not blanking the mind, but letting thoughts arise without being bound, attached, or fixed by them. He also held that 'meditation and wisdom are one,' that 'the afflictions are themselves bodhi' (delusion and awakening are not two things), and that the teaching is 'not established on words' — the deepest truth lies not in scripture's phrases but in what one verifies directly in one's own mind. This style, pointing straight at the human heart and close to daily life, let Chan take genuine root in China.

assessments.text: 受慧能弟子神会之托撰《六祖能禅师碑铭》，是现存最早的慧能传记文献之一，推尊其为南宗正脉。
作为其弟子北上力争，在滑台大会上确立慧能南宗为禅门正统、神秀北宗为旁支，奠定后世禅宗谱系。

assessments_en.text: At the request of Huineng's disciple Shenhui, wrote the 'Stele Inscription for Chan Master Neng,' one of the earliest surviving biographical records of Huineng, honouring him as the true line of the Southern school.

As his disciple, went north to press his case, establishing at the Huatai debate that Huineng's Southern school was the orthodox line of Chan and Shenxiu's Northern school a collateral branch, fixing the later Chan lineage.

quotes: 菩提本无树，明镜亦非台，本来无一物，何处惹尘埃。
不是风动，不是幡动，仁者心动。
何期自性，本自清净；何期自性，本自具足。
quotes_en: Bodhi is originally no tree, nor is the bright mirror a stand; from the first not one thing exists — where could the dust alight?
It is not the wind that moves, nor the flag that moves; it is your minds, good sirs, that move.
Who would have thought that one's own nature is originally pure; who would have thought that one's own nature is originally complete.
works_en: The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch (recorded by his disciple Fahai and others)
huineng.lineage: 上承菩提达摩东来一脉：达摩—慧可—僧璨—道信—弘忍—慧能，为禅宗六祖；下开南宗，经其弟子分衍出临济、曹洞、沩仰、云门、法眼五家七宗，主导此后中国禅乃至日本、朝鲜禅的走向。
huineng.lineage_en: He stood in the line brought east by Bodhidharma — Bodhidharma, Huike, Sengcan, Daoxin, Hongren, Huineng — as the Sixth Patriarch of Chan; and he founded the Southern school, whose branches through his disciples became the 'five houses and seven schools' (Linji, Caodong, Guiyang, Yunmen, Fayan), shaping the later course of Chan in China and of Zen in Japan and Korea.
huineng.trivia: 他出身贫寒、据传不识字，却成为一代宗师，这本身就颠覆了『佛法须靠饱读经卷』的成见，也呼应了他『不立文字、直指人心』的主张。相传其肉身不坏，至今供奉于广东韶关南华寺，成为信众朝拜的圣迹。
huineng.trivia_en: That a man of poor birth, said to be illiterate, should become a great patriarch was itself a rebuke to the assumption that the Dharma must rest on wide reading of scripture — fittingly echoing his own teaching of 'not established on words, pointing straight at the human heart.' His body is said to have remained incorrupt and is enshrined to this day at Nanhua Temple in Shaoguan, Guangdong, a site of pilgrimage for the faithful.

haidt.bio: 1963–，美国社会心理学家，纽约大学斯特恩商学院教授。早年研究道德的心理基础，提出「道德基础理论」；后转向公共议题，先后写出《娇惯的心灵》与《焦虑的一代》，成为讨论青少年心理健康、社交媒体与大学文化的重要声音。
haidt.bio_en: Born 1963, an American social psychologist and professor at New York University's Stern School of Business. He began by studying the psychological roots of morality, proposing "moral foundations theory," then turned to public debates, writing The Coddling of the American Mind and The Anxious Generation, and becoming a leading voice on youth mental health, social media, and campus culture.
haidt.ideas:
海特最想纠正一个流行的误会：我们以为道德判断是先讲道理、再下结论的。其实多数时候恰恰相反——我们先有了一个直觉上的好恶（这事让我恶心、让我愤怒），然后大脑才忙着替这个直觉编理由。他用一个绝妙的比喻概括：人心里住着「大象」和「骑象人」。大象是庞大的、瞬间反应的情感直觉，骑象人是事后讲道理的理性。我们总以为是骑象人在指挥，可真正决定方向的，往往是那头大象——骑象人更像它雇来的辩护律师，专门为大象已经做出的选择找漂亮说辞。
基于此，他提出了「道德基础理论」。他发现人类的道德感不是单一的，而是建立在几根先天的「味蕾」上，就像舌头能尝出酸甜苦咸一样。这些基础大致包括：关爱（不忍他人受苦）、公平（厌恶欺骗与占便宜）、忠诚（对群体的归属）、权威（对秩序与传统的尊重）、圣洁（对纯净与神圣的在意，厌恶亵渎），以及后来补充的自由（反抗压迫）。他的关键洞见是：政治上的左派主要靠前两根味蕾（关爱、公平）来品尝道德，而保守派六根味蕾都用得比较均衡。这解释了为什么左右两派常常鸡同鸭讲——他们不是一方有道德、一方没道德，而是在用不同的味觉系统品尝同一件事，彼此都觉得对方在乎的东西莫名其妙。
近年他把目光转向年轻人。在《娇惯的心灵》里，他和合著者诊断出三个流行却有害的「人生谬见」：凡是伤害你的就让你更脆弱（其实人像免疫系统，适度的挑战才能变强）；永远相信你的感觉（可感觉常常骗人）；人生是好人与坏人的斗争（把复杂分歧简化成善恶对决）。他认为，出于好意却过度的保护——他称之为「安全主义」——正在让一代人把「情感上的不适」误当成「真正的危险」，反而剥夺了他们在磨砺中成长的机会。
在《焦虑的一代》里，他给出了一个更尖锐的论断：大约 2010 年后，青少年的焦虑、抑郁与自残急剧上升，时间点恰好对上智能手机普及和「玩耍式童年」被「手机式童年」取代。孩子们不再在外面摸爬滚打、自己解决冲突，而是低头泡在为成年人设计的、充满比较和成瘾机制的屏幕世界里。他主张推迟给孩子智能手机、把社交媒体挡在高中之外、把更多自由玩耍还给童年。海特的研究因此既是学术，也是一场公共倡议——他相信，理解大象，才能更好地引导它。
haidt.ideas_en:
Haidt's first aim is to correct a popular misconception: we assume moral judgment works by reasoning first and concluding second. In fact it's usually the reverse—we have a gut reaction first (this disgusts me, this enrages me), and only then does the mind busily invent reasons for it. He captures this with a brilliant image: inside each of us live an "elephant" and a "rider." The elephant is the huge, instant emotional intuition; the rider is the reasoning that comes afterward. We imagine the rider is in charge, but the elephant usually sets the direction—the rider is more like its hired lawyer, finding eloquent justifications for choices the elephant has already made.
On this basis he proposed "moral foundations theory." He found that the human moral sense isn't one thing but rests on several innate "taste buds," much as the tongue tastes sweet, sour, bitter, and salty. These foundations roughly include: care (recoiling from others' suffering), fairness (loathing cheating and free-riding), loyalty (belonging to a group), authority (respect for order and tradition), sanctity (caring about purity and the sacred, revulsion at desecration), and a later addition, liberty (resistance to oppression). His key insight: the political left mainly tastes morality with the first two buds (care and fairness), while conservatives use all six more evenly. This explains why left and right so often talk past each other—it's not that one side has morals and the other doesn't, but that they taste the same issue with different palates, each baffled by what the other cares about.
In recent years he turned to the young. In The Coddling of the American Mind, he and his coauthor diagnose three popular but harmful "untruths": that what doesn't kill you makes you weaker (in fact people are like the immune system—moderate challenge is what makes us stronger); always trust your feelings (yet feelings often deceive); and that life is a battle between good people and evil people (collapsing complex disagreements into a clash of good versus evil). He argues that well-meaning but excessive protection—which he calls "safetyism"—is teaching a generation to mistake "emotional discomfort" for "genuine danger," robbing them of the chance to grow through being tested.
In The Anxious Generation he makes a sharper claim: after roughly 2010, adolescent anxiety, depression, and self-harm rose steeply, and the timing lines up with the spread of smartphones and the replacement of a "play-based childhood" by a "phone-based childhood." Children no longer scuffle outdoors and settle their own conflicts, but stare into a screen world built for adults, full of comparison and addictive design. He calls for delaying smartphones, keeping social media out of childhood until high school, and returning more free play to children. Haidt's work is therefore both scholarship and public advocacy—he believes that understanding the elephant is what lets us guide it better.

assessments.text: 该理论被广泛用于解释政治分歧，影响深远；但也有研究者质疑其「基础」的数目与跨文化普适性。
其「手机致青少年心理危机」论引发热烈讨论与政策回响，同时也有心理学家提醒：现有证据多为相关而非因果，不宜把复杂成因单一归咎于屏幕。

assessments_en.by: Scholarly reception of moral foundations theory
assessments_en.text: The theory is widely used to explain political division and has been highly influential; some researchers, however, question the exact number of "foundations" and how universal they are across cultures.

Its claim that phones drove a teen mental-health crisis sparked vigorous debate and policy interest, but some psychologists caution that much of the evidence is correlational rather than causal, and that a complex problem should not be pinned on screens alone.

quotes: 「为孩子准备好道路，而不是为道路准备好孩子。」（海特推广的一句谚语，《娇惯的心灵》）
道德把人凝聚起来，也使人盲目。（《正义之心》）
quotes_en: "Prepare the child for the road, not the road for the child." (a proverb popularized by Haidt, The Coddling of the American Mind)
Morality binds and blinds. (The Righteous Mind)
works: 《娇惯的心灵》(The Coddling of the American Mind，与卢基阿诺夫合著)
works_en: The Coddling of the American Mind (with Greg Lukianoff)
haidt.lineage: 承社会直觉主义与进化心理学；受休谟「理性是激情的奴隶」启发；其工作影响公共舆论、家长运动与多国关于校园手机的政策辩论。
haidt.lineage_en: He builds on social intuitionism and evolutionary psychology, inspired by Hume's claim that "reason is the slave of the passions"; his work has shaped public opinion, parent movements, and policy debates in several countries over phones in schools.
haidt.trivia: 「象与骑象人」的比喻最初出现在他更早的著作《象与骑象人》中，后来成为他全部思想的标志性意象；他长期公开自己的数据与异见者的反驳，把围绕《焦虑的一代》的争论做成了持续更新的公开文档。
haidt.trivia_en: The elephant-and-rider metaphor first appeared in his earlier book The Happiness Hypothesis and later became the signature image of all his thought; he publicly posts his data alongside critics' rebuttals, turning the debate over The Anxious Generation into a continually updated open document.

dweck.bio: 1946–，美国社会与发展心理学家，斯坦福大学教授。数十年研究人们如何看待自己的能力，提出广为人知的「成长型思维」与「固定型思维」之分，著有畅销书《终身成长》(Mindset)。
dweck.bio_en: Born 1946, an American social and developmental psychologist and professor at Stanford University. After decades studying how people view their own abilities, she proposed the widely known distinction between a "growth mindset" and a "fixed mindset," and wrote the best-selling book Mindset.
dweck.ideas:
德韦克一生追问一个看似简单的问题：当人遇到失败和挫折时，为什么有人一蹶不振，有人却越挫越勇？她的答案落在一个字上——你怎么看待「能力」本身。她发现人们大体持有两种信念。一种是「固定型思维」：认为聪明、才华是天生注定、基本不会变的一块固定的量，你要么有、要么没有。另一种是「成长型思维」：相信能力像肌肉，可以通过努力、策略和练习一点点长出来。
这两种信念，会把同一次失败导向截然不同的方向。抱着固定型思维的人，会把每一次考试、每一个挑战都当成对「我到底行不行」的终极审判。所以他们怕失败——因为失败等于证明了「我不够聪明」，这太可怕了，于是他们倾向于回避挑战、一遇困难就放弃、把别人的成功看成对自己的威胁。而抱着成长型思维的人，把失败看成信息和台阶：这次没做好，说明我还没学会、方法还得调，那就再试、再改。挑战对他们不是审判，而是变强的机会。
德韦克最有名的发现，来自她对「表扬」的研究，这个结论颠覆了很多家长和老师的直觉。她让孩子做完一道题后给予表扬，一组夸「你真聪明」，另一组夸「你真努力」。结果，被夸「聪明」的孩子后来更倾向于选简单的题（怕难题搞砸了「聪明」的人设）、遇挫后表现下滑、甚至会谎报成绩；而被夸「努力」的孩子更愿意挑战难题、更享受过程、越挫越韧。这说明：夸什么，就是在悄悄告诉孩子「什么才重要」。夸天赋，养出的是脆弱；夸过程，养出的是韧性。
她把这套思想浓缩成一个温暖的小词——「尚未」(yet)。当一个学生说「我不会解这道题」，固定型思维到此为止；但只要在后面加上一个「尚未」——「我还不会解这道题」——整句话的意味就全变了：它把一扇关闭的门，重新打开成一条仍在延伸的路。失败不再是「我就是不行」，而是「我还在路上」。
需要诚实补充的是：成长型思维的影响近年也经历了科学的检验与争论。一些大规模复制研究发现，它对学业成绩的实际提升往往比早期宣传的要小，且高度依赖如何落地实施——简单地把口号贴在墙上并不管用。德韦克本人也批评过被滥用的「假成长型思维」。但她最核心的洞见依然站得住：我们对「能力是死的还是活的」这一信念，会实实在在地塑造我们面对困难时的勇气。
dweck.ideas_en:
Dweck spent her career on a deceptively simple question: when people hit failure and setbacks, why do some collapse while others come back stronger? Her answer rests on one thing—how you view "ability" itself. She found people tend to hold one of two beliefs. One is a "fixed mindset": the idea that intelligence and talent are an inborn, basically unchangeable quantity—you either have it or you don't. The other is a "growth mindset": the belief that ability is like a muscle, something you can grow bit by bit through effort, strategy, and practice.
These two beliefs send the very same failure in opposite directions. People with a fixed mindset treat every test and every challenge as a final verdict on whether "I've got it or not." So they fear failure—because failing means proving "I'm not smart enough," which is unbearable—and they tend to avoid challenges, give up when things get hard, and see others' success as a threat. People with a growth mindset treat failure as information and a stepping stone: I didn't do well this time, which means I haven't learned it yet and need to adjust, so I'll try again. A challenge isn't a verdict but a chance to get stronger.
Dweck's most famous finding came from her research on praise, and it overturned the intuitions of many parents and teachers. After children finished a task, one group was praised as "so smart," another as "working so hard." The children praised for being "smart" later tended to pick easier problems (afraid a hard one would dent the "smart" image), did worse after a setback, and some even lied about their scores; the children praised for "effort" were more willing to tackle hard problems, enjoyed the process more, and were more resilient. The lesson: what you praise quietly tells a child what matters. Praise talent and you grow fragility; praise process and you grow resilience.
She distilled all this into one warm little word—"yet." When a student says "I can't solve this problem," the fixed mindset stops there; but add a single "yet"—"I can't solve this problem yet"—and the whole sentence changes meaning: a closed door reopens into a road still stretching ahead. Failure is no longer "I just can't do it," but "I'm still on the way."
In fairness it must be added that the impact of growth mindset has lately undergone scientific testing and debate. Some large replication studies found its real boost to academic achievement is often smaller than early publicity suggested and depends heavily on how it is implemented—simply pinning the slogan on a wall doesn't work. Dweck herself has criticized a misused "false growth mindset." Yet her core insight still holds: our belief about whether ability is fixed or alive genuinely shapes the courage we bring to difficulty.

assessments.text: 「成长型思维」被全球无数学校采纳，成为当代教育与育儿话语中影响最广的概念之一。
多项大规模复制研究显示，思维干预对成绩的平均效应较小且依赖实施方式；批评者提醒勿将其当作万能药，德韦克本人亦呼应这一警示。

assessments_en.text: "Growth mindset" has been adopted by countless schools worldwide and become one of the most widely influential ideas in modern education and parenting discourse.

Several large replication studies show the average effect of mindset interventions on grades is small and depends on implementation; critics warn against treating it as a cure-all, a caution Dweck herself echoes.

quotes: 「还不会」(not yet) 这个词，里面藏着通向未来的路。（TED 演讲《相信你能进步的力量》大意）
成为最好的自己，靠的不是与生俱来的天赋，而是终身的努力与学习。（《终身成长》大意）
quotes_en: The words "not yet" contain a path into the future. (paraphrased from her TED talk "The Power of Believing That You Can Improve")
Becoming the best version of yourself comes not from inborn talent but from lifelong effort and learning. (Mindset, paraphrased)
works: 《终身成长》(Mindset: The New Psychology of Success)
TED 演讲《相信你能进步的力量》
works_en: Mindset: The New Psychology of Success
TED talk "The Power of Believing That You Can Improve"
dweck.lineage: 承归因理论与社会认知传统；其思想影响教育心理学、组织管理与体育训练，并与安杰拉·达克沃斯的「坚毅」(grit) 等研究相呼应。
dweck.lineage_en: Building on attribution theory and the social-cognitive tradition, her ideas shaped educational psychology, organizational management, and athletic coaching, and resonate with research such as Angela Duckworth's "grit."
dweck.trivia: 她的成名实验正是给孩子做完题后分别夸「聪明」或「努力」，发现一句表扬就能左右孩子日后是迎难而上还是畏难退缩；后来她也公开批评把口号当摆设的「假成长型思维」。
dweck.trivia_en: Her landmark experiment was exactly the one where children, after finishing a task, were praised either for being "smart" or for "working hard," revealing that a single line of praise can tilt whether a child later faces difficulty or shrinks from it; she later publicly criticized a "false growth mindset" that treats the slogan as mere decoration.

gopnik.bio: 1955–，美国发展心理学家与心智哲学家，加州大学伯克利分校教授。她把婴幼儿当作严肃的科学研究对象，提出孩子其实是天生的「小科学家」，著有《摇篮里的科学家》《宝宝也是哲学家》《园丁与木匠》等。
gopnik.bio_en: Born 1955, an American developmental psychologist and philosopher of mind, a professor at the University of California, Berkeley. Treating infants and toddlers as serious objects of scientific study, she argued that children are born "little scientists," and wrote The Scientist in the Crib, The Philosophical Baby, and The Gardener and the Carpenter.
gopnik.ideas:
高普尼克颠覆了我们对婴儿的看法。在很长一段时间里，人们以为小宝宝只是一团混沌、被动的小肉球，什么都不懂。她却用巧妙的实验证明：婴儿其实是宇宙里最强大的学习机器，是天生的科学家。她提出「理论理论」——意思是，孩子理解世界的方式，和科学家做研究惊人地相似：他们心里悄悄建立起一套关于「事物如何运作」的小小理论，然后通过观察、实验（比如反复把勺子摔到地上看会怎样）、收集证据，不断修正这套理论。
更精确地说，她和同事发现孩子是「贝叶斯学习者」。「贝叶斯」是一种推理方式，听起来高深，其实很贴近常识：你心里先有个大致的猜测，然后每来一条新证据，就按它的分量去调整这个猜测的可信度。孩子正是这样——他们不是被动接收信息，而是像小统计学家一样，从身边纷繁的现象里推断出隐藏的因果规律：按这个按钮灯会亮，那是不是按那个也会亮？他们甚至能从很少的几个例子里，归纳出相当聪明的结论，这种能力至今让研究人工智能的人羡慕不已。
她还提出一个迷人的对比：孩子的意识，可能和大人很不一样。大人的注意力像「聚光灯」(spotlight)——高度聚焦，把光打在一件要紧的事上，周围一切都暗下去，这让我们高效，但也视野狭窄。婴幼儿的意识则更像「灯笼」(lantern)——光向四面八方均匀散开，同时朦胧地觉知到周遭的一切。这就是为什么小孩容易分心，却也常常注意到大人完全忽略的细节；他们活在一种更鲜活、更弥漫的体验里，仿佛时时都在「初次见到世界」。
由此她区分了人生两种根本的学习模式：「探索」与「利用」。「利用」是用好你已经掌握的本领去高效达成目标，那是成年人擅长的；「探索」则是漫无目的地东摸西看、试遍各种可能，哪怕大多没用。童年那看似浪费时间的疯玩、好奇和异想天开，其实是大自然精心安排的「探索期」——孩子的大脑格外柔软可塑，正是要趁这段时间海量地试错、尽情地学，为漫长的一生储备应变的能力。
这也通向她最有名的育儿主张，见于《园丁与木匠》。她说，做父母不该像「木匠」——心里先有张图纸，要把孩子刨削、敲打成某个预定的成品。而该像「园丁」——你的任务是营造一片肥沃、安全、丰富的土壤，然后让每颗种子按自己的天性，长成它本该长成的、你无法预先设计的样子。爱孩子，不是把他打造成某种产品，而是给他一个能茁壮生长的环境。这背后是一个深刻而谦卑的信念：童年的「不成熟」不是缺陷，而是人类最宝贵的发明。
gopnik.ideas_en:
Gopnik overturned how we see babies. For a long time people assumed an infant was just a blob of confusion, a passive lump that understood nothing. With ingenious experiments she showed the opposite: babies are the most powerful learning machines in the universe, born scientists. She proposed the "theory theory"—the idea that the way children make sense of the world is strikingly like what scientists do in research: they quietly build little theories about "how things work," then test them through observation and experiment (dropping a spoon again and again to see what happens) and revise those theories as evidence comes in.
More precisely, she and her colleagues found children are "Bayesian learners." "Bayesian" is a way of reasoning that sounds technical but is really close to common sense: you start with a rough guess, and with each new piece of evidence you adjust how much you believe it, weighted by how strong that evidence is. That is exactly what children do—not passively absorbing information but, like tiny statisticians, inferring the hidden causal rules behind the buzzing world around them: pressing this button makes the light come on, so will pressing that one? They can even draw remarkably smart conclusions from just a few examples, an ability that still leaves artificial-intelligence researchers envious.
She also offered a captivating contrast: a child's consciousness may be very different from an adult's. Adult attention is like a "spotlight"—tightly focused, throwing its beam on the one thing that matters while everything around dims; this makes us efficient but narrow. A young child's consciousness is more like a "lantern"—light spreading evenly in all directions, dimly aware of everything at once. This is why small children are easily distracted yet often notice details adults miss entirely; they live in a more vivid, diffuse experience, as if forever "seeing the world for the first time."
From this she distinguished two fundamental modes of learning: "exploration" and "exploitation." "Exploitation" is using the skills you already have to reach a goal efficiently—what adults are good at. "Exploration" is poking around aimlessly, trying every possibility, even though most lead nowhere. Childhood's seemingly time-wasting wild play, curiosity, and flights of fancy are in fact a carefully arranged "exploration period": the child's brain is especially soft and plastic precisely so that, during this window, it can make a vast number of mistakes and learn to the full, stocking up the adaptability needed for a long life.
This leads to her most famous parenting argument, in The Gardener and the Carpenter. Being a parent, she says, should not be like being a "carpenter"—starting with a blueprint and planing and hammering the child into a predetermined product. It should be like being a "gardener"—your job is to create rich, safe, varied soil, then let each seed grow, according to its own nature, into what it was meant to be, in ways you could never design in advance. To love a child is not to build them into a particular product but to give them an environment in which they can thrive. Behind this lies a deep and humble conviction: childhood's "immaturity" is not a defect but humanity's most precious invention.

assessments.text: 她被视为把贝叶斯与计算模型引入婴幼儿认知研究的开拓者之一，深刻改变了人们对早期心智的理解。
她关于「孩子如何从极少样本中高效学习」的工作，被许多 AI 学者视为对机器学习的重要启发与对照。

assessments_en.text: She is regarded as one of the pioneers who brought Bayesian and computational models into the study of infant cognition, profoundly changing how we understand the early mind.
Her work on how children learn so efficiently from very few examples is seen by many AI scholars as an important inspiration for, and contrast to, machine learning.

quotes: 为人父母不该是一种「工作」，而像是一种爱——你不是在制造某种产品，而是在照料一座花园。（《园丁与木匠》大意）
婴儿和幼儿，也许是人类中最善于思考、最富想象力的成员。（《宝宝也是哲学家》大意）
quotes_en: Being a parent shouldn't be a kind of "work" but a kind of love—you aren't manufacturing a product, you are tending a garden. (The Gardener and the Carpenter, paraphrased)
Babies and young children may be the most thoughtful and imaginative members of our species. (The Philosophical Baby, paraphrased)
works: 《摇篮里的科学家》(The Scientist in the Crib，合著)
《园丁与木匠》(The Gardener and the Carpenter)
gopnik.lineage: 承皮亚杰的认知发展传统，又以贝叶斯与计算建模加以革新；横跨发展心理学与心智哲学，影响早期教育理念与人工智能对人类学习的研究。
gopnik.lineage_en: She builds on Piaget's tradition of cognitive development while renewing it with Bayesian and computational modeling; spanning developmental psychology and philosophy of mind, she has influenced early-education thinking and AI research on human learning.
gopnik.trivia: 她是作家、《纽约客》撰稿人亚当·高普尼克(Adam Gopnik)的姐姐，出身一个人才辈出的知识分子大家庭；她坚持「园丁」式育儿的主张，部分也源于自己养育孩子、含饴弄孙的亲身体会。
gopnik.trivia_en: She is the sister of the writer and New Yorker essayist Adam Gopnik, and comes from a large, intellectually accomplished family; her commitment to "gardener"-style parenting grew in part from her own experience raising children and delighting in grandchildren.

adamsmith.bio: 1723–1790，苏格兰道德哲学家与经济学家，被尊为「现代经济学之父」。他不仅写了奠定经济学的《国富论》，还写了探讨人类道德与同情的《道德情操论》——两本书合起来，才是完整的斯密。
adamsmith.bio_en: 1723–1790, a Scottish moral philosopher and economist honored as the "father of modern economics." He wrote not only The Wealth of Nations, which founded economics, but also The Theory of Moral Sentiments, on human morality and sympathy—and only the two books together give us the whole Smith.
adamsmith.ideas:
提起亚当·斯密，多数人只记得「看不见的手」。这个比喻的意思是：在市场里，每个人都只顾自己的利益——面包师烤面包不是为了行善，而是为了赚钱养家——但奇妙的是，无数这样自利的行为，竟会像被一只「看不见的手」引导着，最终汇成对整个社会有益的结果：面包师为了赚你的钱，就得烤出又好又便宜的面包，于是你也得了好处。他那句名言一针见血：「我们的晚餐并非来自屠夫、酿酒师或面包师的善心，而是出于他们对自身利益的考量。」
他还揭示了财富增长的一大秘密——「分工」。《国富论》开篇就举了个著名例子：做一根别针，如果一个人从头到尾全包，一天做不了几根；可要是把工序拆开，一个人拉铁丝、一个人切断、一个人磨尖、一个人装针头……同样几个工人，一天能做出成千上万根。分工之所以神奇，是因为专注做一件事让人越来越熟练、省去了切换的时间、还容易催生改进工具的发明。现代工厂、乃至整个全球供应链，背后都是这个朴素而强大的道理。
但若只记住这些，就大大误读了斯密。他首先是位道德哲学家。在更早的《道德情操论》里，他追问：人明明自私，为什么还会关心他人、还有道德？他的答案是「同情」（更准确说是「共感」）——我们天生能在想象中设身处地，体会别人的喜怒哀乐。在此基础上他提出了一个极美的概念：「公正的旁观者」。当你要判断自己的行为是否正当时，仿佛心里住着一位冷静、不偏不倚的旁观者，正从外部看着你；你会不自觉地问：一个明事理的外人，会赞许还是谴责我现在做的事？这个内心的旁观者，就是良心的来源。所以在斯密看来，自利从来不等于自私无度——真正的市场社会，是建立在同情、信任与道德约束之上的。
他甚至清醒地看到了自己所赞美的分工的「阴暗面」。他警告说：一个人若一辈子只重复几个极其简单的动作（比如一天到晚只磨别针尖），他的头脑会变得迟钝麻木，渐渐失去思考、判断和关心公共事务的能力——分工在提高效率的同时，可能让工人「变蠢」。正因如此，他主张国家应当出面提供基础教育，来对冲这种损害。这份对普通劳动者命运的关切，与今天人们担忧流水线、外卖算法把人异化的讨论，遥相呼应。
所以，真正的斯密远比「自由市场代言人」这个标签丰富。他一手画出了市场如何高效运转，另一手又时刻提醒：市场必须扎根于道德情感与公正之心，否则便会走向贪婪与失序。读懂了《道德情操论》与《国富论》两本书的人，才算认识了完整的他。
adamsmith.ideas_en:
Mention Adam Smith and most people remember only the "invisible hand." The image means this: in a market, everyone pursues only their own interest—the baker bakes bread not out of charity but to earn a living—yet remarkably, countless such self-interested acts, as if guided by an "invisible hand," add up to an outcome that benefits society as a whole: to win your money, the baker must bake good, cheap bread, and so you gain too. His famous line cuts to the heart of it: "It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest."
He also revealed a great secret of growing wealth—the "division of labor." The Wealth of Nations opens with a famous example: making a pin. If one person does the whole job alone, they can make only a few a day; but split the steps—one draws the wire, one cuts it, one sharpens it, one fits the head—and the same handful of workers can make tens of thousands a day. Division of labor works such wonders because focusing on one task makes a person ever more skilled, saves the time of switching, and tends to spark inventions that improve the tools. Modern factories, and indeed the whole global supply chain, run on this plain but powerful truth.
But to remember only this is to badly misread Smith. He was first of all a moral philosopher. In his earlier The Theory of Moral Sentiments he asks: if people are selfish, why do they still care about others and possess morality at all? His answer is "sympathy" (more precisely, fellow-feeling)—we are by nature able, in imagination, to put ourselves in another's place and feel their joys and sorrows. On this he built a beautiful idea: the "impartial spectator." When you judge whether your own conduct is right, it is as if a calm, even-handed onlooker lived within you, watching from the outside; you can't help asking: would a sensible stranger approve or condemn what I'm doing now? That inner spectator is the source of conscience. So for Smith self-interest was never the same as boundless selfishness—a true market society rests on sympathy, trust, and moral restraint.
He even saw clearly the dark side of the very division of labor he praised. He warned: if a person spends a lifetime repeating a few extremely simple motions (sharpening pin-points all day long), his mind grows dull and numb, gradually losing the capacity to think, to judge, and to care about public affairs—division of labor, while raising efficiency, can make the worker "stupid." For just this reason he argued the state should step in to provide basic education to offset the harm. This concern for the fate of ordinary laborers echoes today's worries that the assembly line and the delivery-app algorithm alienate the people who work them.
So the real Smith is far richer than the label "spokesman for the free market." With one hand he sketched how markets work so efficiently; with the other he never stopped warning that markets must be rooted in moral sentiment and a sense of justice, or they slide into greed and disorder. Only those who have read both The Theory of Moral Sentiments and The Wealth of Nations have met the whole man.

assessments.text: 他被普遍尊为「现代经济学之父」，《国富论》被视为系统政治经济学的奠基之作。
十九世纪学者曾争论《道德情操论》的「同情」与《国富论》的「自利」是否矛盾；当代研究多认为二者实为一以贯之、互补的整体。

assessments_en.text: He is widely honored as the "father of modern economics," and The Wealth of Nations is seen as the founding work of systematic political economy.

Nineteenth-century scholars argued over whether the "sympathy" of Moral Sentiments contradicts the "self-interest" of The Wealth of Nations; most modern scholarship sees the two as a single, complementary whole.

quotes: 我们的晚餐并非来自屠夫、酿酒师或面包师的善心，而是出于他们对自身利益的考量。（《国富论》）
无论人被认为多么自私，他的天性中显然还有一些本能，使他关心他人的命运。（《道德情操论》开篇）
quotes_en: It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest. (The Wealth of Nations)
How selfish soever man may be supposed, there are evidently some principles in his nature which interest him in the fortune of others. (opening of The Theory of Moral Sentiments)
works: 《国富论》(An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations)
《道德情操论》(The Theory of Moral Sentiments)
works_en: The Wealth of Nations (An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations)
adamsmith.lineage: 承苏格兰启蒙运动，与休谟是挚友；师从哈奇森。其思想奠定古典经济学，启发李嘉图、马尔萨斯，并持续滋养至今的自由市场理论与道德哲学讨论。
adamsmith.lineage_en: A product of the Scottish Enlightenment and a close friend of David Hume, he studied under Francis Hutcheson. His thought laid the foundation of classical economics, inspired Ricardo and Malthus, and still nourishes both free-market theory and moral philosophy today.
adamsmith.trivia: 斯密以心不在焉、沉于沉思闻名：据传他曾一边构思一边把面包黄油泡进茶里，还说这是他喝过最难喝的茶；又有说他穿着睡袍出门散步，神游间走出十几英里才回过神。
adamsmith.trivia_en: Smith was famous for his absent-mindedness and deep abstraction: he is said to have once, lost in thought, dropped buttered bread into his tea and pronounced it the worst cup he'd ever had; another tale has him strolling out in his dressing gown and walking some fifteen miles in a reverie before coming to his senses.

hanfeizi.bio: 约前280–前233，战国末期韩国公子，法家思想的集大成者。他口吃、不善言辞，却长于著书；与李斯同师事荀子。其著作传入秦国，秦王嬴政读《孤愤》《五蠹》后惊叹『嗟乎，寡人得见此人与之游，死不恨矣』。后韩非奉命使秦，被同门李斯妒忌进谗，下狱，死于狱中。他本人不得善终，思想却为秦统一六国提供了理论骨架，并经历代『外儒内法』深刻塑造了中国的治理传统。
hanfeizi.bio_en: c. 280–233 BC, a prince of the state of Han in the late Warring States period and the great synthesizer of Legalist thought. He stammered and was a poor speaker but a brilliant writer; he and Li Si both studied under Xunzi. When his writings reached the state of Qin, King Zheng (the future First Emperor) read his essays 'Solitary Indignation' and 'The Five Vermin' and sighed, 'Ah! If I could meet this man and befriend him, I could die without regret.' Sent later as an envoy to Qin, Han Fei was slandered out of jealousy by his fellow student Li Si, imprisoned, and died in jail. He met a wretched end, yet his thought gave the theoretical skeleton for Qin's unification of China and, through the later tradition of 'Confucian outside, Legalist inside,' shaped Chinese statecraft for two thousand years.
hanfeizi.ideas:
韩非子要回答的是一个极现实的问题：在人人都为自己打算的乱世里，怎样才能让一个组织（国家）稳定、高效、不靠运气地运转？他的答案冷峻而清醒——别指望人人都是圣贤，要靠制度。
他先立一个前提：人性趋利避害。他不像孟子那样相信人性本善，而是更务实地说，人做事的根本动机是计算利害。父母对子女尚且会因『将来谁养老』而权衡，君臣之间更是一场赤裸的利益交换。所以想靠『感化』『恩义』让人长久效力是靠不住的——靠不住的不是道德本身，而是把整个治理建立在少数人偶然的德性上。
于是他提出治理三件套：法、术、势。『法』是公开、明确、人人可知可循的规则与赏罚，关键在一个『信』字——说赏就一定赏、说罚就一定罚，且不分贵贱（『刑过不避大臣，赏善不遗匹夫』）。法越透明，人越能预期，就越不必看长官的好恶脸色。『术』是君主考核、驾驭臣下的手段，核心是『循名责实』——你担什么职、夸口要做成什么，就拿实际结果来对照，名实相符才赏，办不成要罚。『势』是位置本身带来的权威：同一句话，君主说出来管用、普通人说出来没人理，差别不在人，在『势』。三者缺一不可：有法无术，君主会被臣下蒙蔽；有术无势，再高明也推不动；有势无法，就成了任性的暴政。
他还反复强调一件被后人误解的事：法家不是教君主任意妄为，恰恰相反，是要君主把自己也关进制度里——『明主治吏不治民』，君主不该事必躬亲去管每个百姓，而是设计好规则与考核、管好各级官吏，让系统自己运转。这其实是一种极早的『靠制度而非靠能人』的组织思想，今天读来仍像在谈大型组织如何用规则和激励替代对个别英雄的依赖。
韩非的局限也很明显：他眼里只有君主与国家的强大，几乎不谈个人的尊严、价值与权利，把人完全当成可赏可罚的工具，这是法家最被后世诟病之处。但他对『人性自利』『制度优于人治』『激励决定行为』的洞察，至今在管理、经济、法律与组织设计里反复被验证——任何想让一群陌生人可靠协作的人，都绕不开他提出的问题。
hanfeizi.ideas_en:
Han Feizi set out to answer a brutally practical question: in a chaotic age where everyone calculates for themselves, how can an organization — a state — run stably, efficiently, and not by luck? His answer is bleak and clear-eyed: do not count on everyone being a sage; rely on institutions.
He begins from a premise: human nature chases gain and flees harm. Unlike Mencius, who trusted that people are good at root, he says more pragmatically that the basic motive behind what people do is a calculation of advantage. Even parents weigh 'who will support me in old age' toward their children; between ruler and minister it is a naked exchange of interests. So relying on 'moral influence' and 'favor and loyalty' to keep people serving you for long is unreliable — and what is unreliable is not morality itself, but founding all of governance on the accidental virtue of a few.
Hence his triad of rule: law, statecraft, and positional power. 'Law' is open, explicit rules of reward and punishment that everyone can know and follow, and its key is reliability — what is promised as reward is always given, what is threatened as punishment always falls, sparing neither high nor low ('punishment does not spare great ministers; reward does not skip the common man'). The more transparent the law, the better people can predict, and the less they must read an official's moods. 'Statecraft' is the ruler's means of appraising and steering his ministers, centered on holding performance to the title — you hold a post and boast what you will accomplish, and your actual results are checked against it; reward only when word matches deed, punish when it does not. 'Positional power' is the authority that comes from the position itself: the same sentence works when a ruler says it and is ignored when an ordinary man does — the difference lies not in the person but in the power of office. None of the three can be missing: law without statecraft, and the ruler is deceived by his ministers; statecraft without positional power, and even the cleverest cannot move things; positional power without law, and you get capricious tyranny.
He also stresses something later ages misread: Legalism does not teach the ruler to act arbitrarily — quite the opposite, it asks the ruler to lock himself, too, inside the system. 'The wise ruler governs the officials, not the people directly': he should not personally manage every commoner but should design good rules and appraisals, govern the officials well, and let the system run itself. This is, in fact, a very early form of organizational thinking that relies on institutions rather than on gifted individuals — read today, it sounds like a discussion of how large organizations use rules and incentives to replace dependence on individual heroes.
His limits are just as plain: he sees only the strength of ruler and state, almost never the dignity, worth, or rights of the individual, and treats people purely as instruments to be rewarded or punished — the aspect of Legalism most condemned by later ages. Yet his insights — that human nature is self-interested, that institutions beat the rule of men, that incentives drive behavior — are confirmed again and again in management, economics, law, and organizational design. Anyone who wants a crowd of strangers to cooperate reliably cannot get around the questions he raised.

assessments.text: 为韩非立传，深惜其虽著《说难》洞悉进谏之难，最终仍因谗言冤死于秦，叹其『悲廉直不容于邪枉之臣』。
读《孤愤》《五蠹》后极为倾倒，叹『得见此人与之游，死不恨矣』；其学说成为秦中央集权制度的理论基础。
多斥法家『刻薄寡恩』、视人为工具、不施仁义教化，并以秦二世而亡为据，认为纯任法术、不行仁政正是速亡之因。

assessments_en.by: Sima Qian, Records of the Grand Historian
assessments_en.text: He gave Han Fei a biography, lamenting that though Han wrote 'The Difficulties of Persuasion' and understood perfectly how hard it is to advise a ruler, he still died wronged in Qin through slander — grieving that 'the upright and honest find no place among crooked, treacherous ministers.'

Bowled over after reading 'Solitary Indignation' and 'The Five Vermin,' he sighed that to meet and befriend this man he 'could die without regret'; Han Fei's doctrine became the theoretical basis of Qin's centralized autocracy.

Largely condemned Legalism as 'harsh and ungenerous,' treating people as tools and refusing benevolent moral education; citing Qin's collapse in a single generation, they held that ruling purely by law and statecraft without benevolent government was the very cause of its swift fall.

quotes: 法不阿贵，绳不挠曲。——法律不偏袒权贵，墨绳不迁就弯曲。（《韩非子·有度》）
宰相必起于州部，猛将必发于卒伍。（《韩非子·显学》）
明主之所导制其臣者，二柄而已矣：刑、德也。——君主驾驭臣下，靠的不过赏与罚两个权柄。（《韩非子·二柄》）
quotes_en: The law does not fawn on the noble; the inked line does not bend to the crooked. (Han Feizi, 'On Having Standards')
A chancellor must rise from the local districts; a fierce general must come up from the ranks. (Han Feizi, 'Eminent Learning')
What a wise ruler uses to guide and control his ministers is nothing but two handles: punishment and reward. (Han Feizi, 'The Two Handles')
hanfeizi.lineage: 师承荀子（『性恶』一脉），综合商鞅之『法』、申不害之『术』、慎到之『势』而集法家大成；其学说由同门李斯付诸实践，塑造了秦的中央集权制度，并经历代『外儒内法』深刻影响中国两千年的治理传统。
hanfeizi.lineage_en: A student of Xunzi (the 'human nature is bad' line), he synthesized Shang Yang's 'law,' Shen Buhai's 'statecraft,' and Shen Dao's 'positional power' into the culmination of Legalism; his doctrine, put into practice by his fellow student Li Si, shaped Qin's centralized autocracy and, through the enduring tradition of 'Confucian outside, Legalist inside,' influenced Chinese statecraft for two millennia.
hanfeizi.trivia: 构陷他的李斯，正是他同出荀子门下的师兄弟。秦王为得韩非不惜发兵攻韩；韩非入秦后却被李斯进谗下狱、冤死——一个被自己学说所成就的帝国，反过来吞噬了它的理论奠基人。
hanfeizi.trivia_en: Li Si, who framed him, was his own fellow student under Xunzi. The King of Qin even sent troops against Han to obtain Han Fei; yet once in Qin, Han Fei was slandered by Li Si, jailed, and died wronged — the empire his doctrine made then devoured the very man who laid its theory.

hayek.bio: 1899–1992，奥地利裔英国经济学家、政治哲学家，奥地利经济学派代表人物，1974 年诺贝尔经济学奖得主。生于维也纳一个学术世家，一战后求学于维也纳大学，师从米塞斯。他先后任教于伦敦政治经济学院、芝加哥大学与弗莱堡大学。在凯恩斯主义席卷世界、计划经济风头正盛的年代，他几乎是逆流而立、长期坐冷板凳；晚年随新自由主义复兴而重获影响，1991 年获美国总统自由勋章。
hayek.bio_en: 1899–1992, an Austrian-British economist and political philosopher, a leading figure of the Austrian School and the 1974 Nobel laureate in economics. Born into a scholarly Viennese family, he studied at the University of Vienna after the First World War under Ludwig von Mises, and went on to teach at the London School of Economics, the University of Chicago, and Freiburg. In an age when Keynesianism swept the world and central planning was in vogue, he stood almost alone against the current, long out of fashion; his thought revived late in life with the resurgence of classical liberalism, and in 1991 he received the U.S. Presidential Medal of Freedom.
hayek.ideas:
哈耶克一生都在回答一个问题：一个没有人能纵观全局的复杂社会，凭什么能有序运转？他的答案颠覆直觉——秩序未必来自设计，最好的秩序恰恰是『没人设计出来的』。
起点是他著名的『知识问题』。我们常以为，只要找一群足够聪明的专家、收集足够多的数据，就能从中央把整个经济计划好。哈耶克说这是幻觉：经济运行所依赖的关键知识根本无法集中。它不是一本可以汇总上交的统计年鉴，而是分散在千百万人手里、且大多『只可意会』的具体知识——这条街哪个时段人流多、这台旧机器哪里爱坏、这个客户其实更在乎交期而非价格。这些知识因时因地不断变化、转瞬即逝，只有身处现场的当事人才掌握；任何中央机构拿到的信息，永远是滞后而残缺的。
那分散的知识怎么协调？靠价格。在哈耶克看来，价格是一套精妙的信号系统：当某种东西变稀缺，价格上涨，无数素不相识、并不需要知道究竟发生了什么的人，会自发地少用它、去找替代、增加供给。一个数字，就把分散在全社会的知识压缩并传递了出去——这就是市场作为『发现程序』的奇迹。
由此他提出『自发秩序』：市场、语言、习俗、普通法这些东西，都不是哪个天才设计的，而是无数人在长期互动中自然演化、相互调适涌现出来的有序格局——『人之行动而非人之设计的产物』。它往往比任何刻意的总体规划更精巧、更能适应变化。
这也是他对计划经济最深的警告，集中在《通往奴役之路》里：全盘计划之所以危险，首先因为它在认识论上不可能（知识无法集中），勉强推行就必然要靠强制——为让计划落地，得不断扩权去压制不服从的个体，于是善意的集权一步步滑向极权。他把这种以为人能凭理性设计整个社会的傲慢，称为『致命的自负』。
但要澄清一个常见误解：哈耶克并非无政府主义者，也不主张丛林法则。他认为政府的核心职责，是维护一套抽象、普遍、对人人平等适用的规则（法治），并在这套规则下让个人自由行动。他反对的不是『规则』，而是那种针对特定结果、不断微操干预的『指挥式』权力。理解这一点，才不会把他简单贴成『市场原教旨主义』。
hayek.ideas_en:
Hayek spent his life on one question: how can a complex society, where no one can survey the whole, ever run in an orderly way? His answer overturns intuition — order need not come from design; the best order is precisely the kind no one designed.
The starting point is his famous 'knowledge problem.' We tend to think that if we gather enough clever experts and enough data, a center can plan the whole economy. Hayek calls this an illusion: the decisive knowledge an economy runs on simply cannot be centralized. It is not a statistical yearbook that can be compiled and handed up, but concrete knowledge scattered among millions and largely tacit — which hours this street is busy, where this old machine tends to fail, that this customer actually cares more about delivery time than price. Such knowledge shifts constantly with time and place and is fleeting; only the person on the spot holds it, and any central body's information is forever lagging and incomplete.
Then how is dispersed knowledge coordinated? Through prices. For Hayek, the price is an exquisite signaling system: when something grows scarce and its price rises, countless strangers — who need not know what actually happened — spontaneously use less of it, seek substitutes, and supply more. A single number compresses and transmits knowledge dispersed across all of society. This is the marvel of the market as a 'discovery procedure.'
From this he derives 'spontaneous order': markets, language, customs, the common law — none of these was designed by some genius; each is an orderly pattern that emerged as countless people interacted, evolved, and mutually adjusted over time — 'the result of human action but not of human design.' It is often more intricate and more adaptive than any deliberate master plan.
This is also his deepest warning against central planning, concentrated in The Road to Serfdom: total planning is dangerous first because it is epistemically impossible (knowledge cannot be centralized), and forcing it through must then rely on coercion — to make the plan stick you must keep expanding power to suppress the noncompliant, so well-meaning centralization slides step by step into totalitarianism. This arrogance — the belief that one can design an entire society by reason — he called 'the fatal conceit.'
But a common misreading must be corrected: Hayek was no anarchist and did not preach the law of the jungle. He held that government's core duty is to maintain a set of abstract, general rules applying equally to all (the rule of law) and to let individuals act freely beneath them. What he opposed is not 'rules' but the 'commanding' kind of power that micromanages toward specific outcomes. Grasp this, and you won't simply tag him a 'market fundamentalist.'

assessments.text: 因『在货币与经济波动理论上的开创性工作，以及对经济、社会与制度现象相互依存的深刻分析』授奖。
读《通往奴役之路》后致信哈耶克，称『在道德与哲学上，我发现自己几乎完全同意』，尽管二人在经济政策上是著名论敌。
认为他低估了市场失灵、信息不对称与权力集中等问题，『价格能传递一切知识』在现实中并不总成立。

assessments_en.text: Awarded for 'pioneering work in the theory of money and economic fluctuations and for penetrating analysis of the interdependence of economic, social, and institutional phenomena.'

After reading The Road to Serfdom he wrote to Hayek that 'morally and philosophically I find myself in agreement with virtually the whole of it' — though the two were famous adversaries on economic policy.
Argue he underrated market failure, information asymmetry, and the concentration of power; that 'prices convey all the knowledge' does not always hold in practice.

quotes: 经济学有一项奇特的任务：向人们揭示，对于他们自以为能够设计的东西，他们实际上知道得何其之少。（《致命的自负》）
国家『计划』得越多，个人的计划就变得越困难。（《通往奴役之路》）
quotes_en: The curious task of economics is to demonstrate to men how little they really know about what they imagine they can design. (The Fatal Conceit)
The more the state 'plans' the more difficult planning becomes for the individual. (The Road to Serfdom)
works: 《个人主义与经济秩序》（含〈知识在社会中的运用〉）
works_en: Individualism and Economic Order (incl. 'The Use of Knowledge in Society')
hayek.lineage: 承自门格尔、米塞斯的奥地利学派，与凯恩斯展开二十世纪最著名的经济学论战；其思想经弗里德曼等芝加哥学派呼应，深刻影响了战后新自由主义与撒切尔、里根的政策，也与波普尔的『开放社会』互为呼应，启发了当代复杂系统与制度经济学。
hayek.lineage_en: Heir to the Austrian School of Menger and Mises, he waged the twentieth century's most famous economics debate with Keynes; echoed by Friedman and the Chicago School, his thought deeply shaped postwar classical liberalism and the policies of Thatcher and Reagan, resonated with Popper's 'open society,' and inspired modern complexity science and institutional economics.
hayek.trivia: 他与凯恩斯虽是论敌，私交却不算坏——二战期间两人甚至曾一同在剑桥国王学院的屋顶值夜、防德军空袭纵火弹。1944 年《通往奴役之路》出乎意料地成为畅销书，《读者文摘》的删节普及版更让他一度在美国声名大噪。
hayek.trivia_en: Though adversaries, he and Keynes were on cordial personal terms — during the Second World War the two even took fire-watch duty together on the roof of King's College, Cambridge, against German incendiary raids. In 1944 The Road to Serfdom unexpectedly became a bestseller, and a condensed Reader's Digest edition briefly made him famous across America.

jensen.bio: 1963 年生于台湾台南，九岁随家移居美国，曾在肯塔基一所招收问题少年的寄宿学校度过一段艰苦时光。俄勒冈州立大学电机工程学士、斯坦福硕士。1993 年与两位伙伴在一家餐厅里创办英伟达（NVIDIA），任首席执行官至今，是科技史上在位最久的创始人 CEO 之一。他带领英伟达从一家几度濒临倒闭的显卡公司，成长为 AI 时代算力的核心供应者、全球市值最高的公司之一，并以标志性的黑色皮夹克闻名。
jensen.bio_en: Born in 1963 in Tainan, Taiwan, he moved to the United States at nine and spent a hard stretch at a Kentucky boarding school that took in troubled boys. He holds a bachelor's in electrical engineering from Oregon State and a master's from Stanford. In 1993 he co-founded NVIDIA with two partners in a diner, and he has been its CEO ever since — one of the longest-serving founder-CEOs in tech history. He led NVIDIA from a graphics-card company that several times nearly went under to the core supplier of compute for the AI era and one of the most valuable companies on earth, famous for his signature black leather jacket.
jensen.ideas:
黄仁勋的思想不写在书里，而是一套从三十年九死一生中淬炼出来的工作信念，核心可拆成几条。
第一，是对『加速计算』的长期押注。早在 AI 热潮之前，他就坚信传统 CPU 一步步串行处理的方式终会触到物理极限，未来属于能同时处理成千上万件小任务的『并行计算』——这正是 GPU（图形处理器）所擅长。他赌的是从图形、科学计算到后来的深度学习，世界会越来越需要这种大规模并行的算力。事实证明，现代 AI、尤其神经网络的训练几乎全靠 GPU，这一押注让英伟达站到了 AI 革命的发动机位置。
第二，是『买得越多，省得越多』的反直觉账。他反复对客户说：看起来昂贵的加速计算硬件，因为把任务做得快得多、能耗效率高得多，综合算下来反而比廉价的传统方案更省钱。这背后是一种算总账、算长期账的思维，而非只盯单次采购的标价。
第三，是『痛苦造就伟大』。他公开说过，不希望员工甚至自己的孩子过得太顺，因为『伟大不来自智慧，而来自苦难与挣扎中锻造出的品格与韧性』。英伟达多次濒死的经历，被他视为公司最宝贵的财富——这是一种把逆境重新定义为养分的心态。
第四，是他独特的组织哲学：极度扁平、极度透明。他有数十位直接下属、不开一对一会议，几乎所有重要信息向全员公开，反对用层层汇报去『保护』高管。他相信把信息摊平、让最有能力的人直接面对真实问题，胜过用科层制去缓冲和过滤——『我希望大家都掌握同样的信息，自己做出最好的判断』。
第五，是亲力亲为的『第一性』工程师本色。即便身为巨头掌门，他仍以钻进技术细节、与工程师直接辩论著称，强调从最根本的物理与原理出发思考，而非依赖二手汇报。几条加在一起，是一个把长期赌注、逆境韧性与透明组织揉在一起的实干者形象。
jensen.ideas_en:
Huang's thinking isn't written in books; it's a set of working convictions forged over thirty years of near-death experiences, and it breaks down into a few strands.
First, a long bet on 'accelerated computing.' Well before the AI boom, he was convinced that the traditional CPU's way of processing one step at a time would eventually hit physical limits, and that the future belonged to 'parallel computing' — handling thousands of small tasks at once, exactly what a GPU (graphics processor) is good at. He bet that from graphics to scientific computing to, later, deep learning, the world would need ever more of this massively parallel compute. He was right: modern AI, especially the training of neural networks, runs almost entirely on GPUs, and that bet put NVIDIA at the engine room of the AI revolution.
Second, the counterintuitive math of 'the more you buy, the more you save.' He tells customers again and again that accelerated-computing hardware, though it looks expensive, gets the work done so much faster and so much more energy-efficiently that, all in, it costs less than cheap traditional gear. Behind this is a habit of counting the total, long-run bill rather than the sticker price of a single purchase.
Third, 'greatness is forged in pain.' He has said publicly that he doesn't want employees — or even his own kids — to have it too easy, because 'greatness comes not from intelligence but from character and resilience forged in suffering and struggle.' NVIDIA's repeated brushes with death he counts as the company's most precious asset — a mindset that redefines adversity as nourishment.
Fourth, his distinctive organizational philosophy: radically flat and radically transparent. He has dozens of direct reports, holds no one-on-ones, keeps nearly all important information open to everyone, and rejects using layers of reporting to 'protect' executives. He believes that flattening information and letting the ablest people face real problems directly beats cushioning and filtering through bureaucracy — 'I want everyone to have the same information and make the best decision themselves.'
Fifth, the hands-on, first-principles engineer at heart. Even as the head of a giant, he is known for diving into technical detail and arguing directly with engineers, insisting on thinking from the most basic physics and principles rather than relying on secondhand reports. Together these make the portrait of a doer who fuses long-horizon bets, resilience under adversity, and a transparent organization.

assessments.text: 将其列为年度全球最具影响力人物之一，称英伟达的芯片是支撑当代人工智能革命的『底层引擎』。
被广泛视为最具远见的科技 CEO 之一，提前十余年押注加速计算与 AI 算力；其在位之久、与公司绑定之深在科技业罕见。
质疑英伟达近乎垄断的市场地位与高定价，以及 AI 算力热潮中潜在的估值泡沫；其『以苦为养』的高压文化亦有争议。

assessments_en.text: Named him among the year's most influential people in the world, calling NVIDIA's chips the 'foundational engine' powering today's AI revolution.

Widely regarded as one of the most visionary tech CEOs, having bet on accelerated computing and AI compute more than a decade early; his tenure and identification with the company are rare in the industry.
Question NVIDIA's near-monopoly position and high pricing, and a possible valuation bubble in the AI-compute frenzy; his 'suffering as nourishment' high-pressure culture is also contested.

quotes: 我们离倒闭永远只有三十天。（黄仁勋常挂嘴边的危机感，大意）
伟大不来自智慧，而来自品格；而品格不是在聪明人身上、是在经受苦难的人身上锻造出来的。（2023 年斯坦福演讲，大意）
买得越多，省得越多。（他推介加速计算时的标志性说法）
quotes_en: We are always thirty days from going out of business. (a sense of crisis Huang often voices; paraphrased)
Greatness comes not from intelligence but from character — and character is forged not in the smart but in those who have suffered. (2023 Stanford address; paraphrased)
The more you buy, the more you save. (his signature line when pitching accelerated computing)
works: 英伟达 CUDA 并行计算平台（2006）
推动 GPU 深度学习生态的奠基
历年 GTC 主题演讲
works_en: Foundational work building the GPU deep-learning ecosystem
jensen.lineage: 工程上深受并行计算与图形学传统影响；与台积电张忠谋、AMD 苏姿丰同属华裔半导体领军群体。他扁平透明的管理哲学，与英特尔安迪·格鲁夫《只有偏执狂才能生存》、亚马逊贝索斯的『Day 1』心态遥相呼应，也常被拿来与乔布斯式的产品独裁相对照。
jensen.lineage_en: Shaped in engineering by the traditions of parallel computing and graphics; he stands with TSMC's Morris Chang and AMD's Lisa Su among the ethnic-Chinese leaders of semiconductors. His flat, transparent management philosophy echoes Intel's Andy Grove (Only the Paranoid Survive) and Amazon's Bezos 'Day 1' mindset, and is often contrasted with Jobs-style product autocracy.
jensen.trivia: 公司名 NVIDIA 取自拉丁语 invidia（嫉妒），寓意让对手『眼红』；当年三位创始人是在加州一家 Denny's 连锁餐厅里敲定创业的——而他少年时正是在 Denny's 端盘子、刷厕所打工。他左臂纹有英伟达 logo，据说是为兑现『股价达标就去纹身』的赌约。
jensen.trivia_en: The name NVIDIA derives from the Latin invidia ('envy'), the idea being to make rivals green with it; the three founders sealed the plan in a Denny's diner in California — the very chain where, as a teenager, Huang had bussed tables and cleaned restrooms. He has the NVIDIA logo tattooed on his arm, reportedly to honor a bet that he'd get inked once the stock hit a target.

dunbar.bio: 1947 年生，英国人类学家、进化心理学家，牛津大学进化心理学荣休教授，曾领导『社会与进化神经科学研究小组』。他以提出『邓巴数』闻名于世——通过比较灵长类大脑新皮层的大小与其社群规模的关系，推算出人类能维持的稳定社会关系上限约为 150。他的研究横跨灵长类行为、人类社会网络、语言与梳毛的演化，以及宗教与笑的社会功能。
dunbar.bio_en: Born in 1947, a British anthropologist and evolutionary psychologist, emeritus professor of evolutionary psychology at Oxford, where he led the Social and Evolutionary Neuroscience Research Group. He is famous for 'Dunbar's number' — by comparing the size of the neocortex in primates with the size of their social groups, he estimated that the upper limit of stable social relationships a human can maintain is about 150. His research spans primate behavior, human social networks, the evolution of language and grooming, and the social functions of religion and laughter.
dunbar.ideas:
邓巴想解开一个谜：为什么灵长类、尤其人类的大脑，那个负责复杂思维的新皮层，长得这么大、这么耗能？他给出的答案是著名的『社会脑假说』——大脑变大，主要不是为了使用工具或找食物，而是为了应对群居生活的复杂：要记住谁是谁、谁跟谁好、谁欠了谁人情、谁上次骗过你……维系一个又大又稳定的社群，是一项极其烧脑的任务，正是这种社交压力推动了智力的进化。
顺着这个思路，他做了个大胆的推算：既然灵长类的社群规模与其新皮层大小高度相关，那把人类的新皮层比例代进去，就能预测人类『天然』的社群规模——算出来约是 150，这就是『邓巴数』：一个人能维持的、有意义且稳定的社会关系的上限。超过它，关系就会『超载』，只能靠规章制度而非私人情谊来维系。这个数字在历史里反复出现：原始部落的典型规模、罗马军队的基本单位、许多公司开始觉得『需要正式管理层』的临界点，都惊人地接近 150。
更实用的是，他指出这 150 不是平的，而是一圈圈同心圆：最里层约 5 个最亲密的人（危难时会求助的），然后约 15 个可深度信任的好友，约 50 个朋友，约 150 个稳定熟人，再外面是约 500 个认识的人、1500 个叫得出名字的人。每往外一层，关系的强度和你愿投入的精力都骤减。
他还有个迷人的『梳毛—语言』假说：猴子靠互相梳毛来结盟、安抚关系，但梳毛一次只能对一个对象，效率太低、撑不起大群体。人类则演化出语言，尤其是『八卦』——聊天就像『用声音梳毛』，能同时安抚好几个人，还能传递『谁可信、谁该防』的社会信息，这才让我们突破梳毛的人数瓶颈、维持起更大的网络。
这些研究对今天有个清醒的提醒：社交媒体让你『好友』上千，却并不能突破大脑的硬约束——你真正在乎、真正维系的，依然是那一小圈人。关系是有成本的、会衰减的，需要时间和面对面的投入去『充值』。认清这一点，反而能帮人把有限的精力，投到真正重要的少数关系上。
dunbar.ideas_en:
Dunbar set out to solve a puzzle: why is the brain of primates — and especially humans — so large and so energy-hungry, particularly the neocortex that handles complex thought? His answer is the famous 'social brain hypothesis': the brain grew large not mainly to use tools or find food but to cope with the complexity of group living — remembering who is who, who is allied with whom, who owes whom a favor, who cheated you last time. Sustaining a large, stable group is an enormously demanding cognitive task, and it was precisely this social pressure that drove the evolution of intelligence.
Following this thread, he made a bold calculation: since group size in primates correlates closely with neocortex size, plugging in the human neocortex ratio should predict our 'natural' group size — and the figure comes out around 150. This is 'Dunbar's number': the upper limit of meaningful, stable social relationships one person can maintain. Beyond it, relationships 'overload' and can only be held together by rules and institutions rather than personal bonds.
