His most famous investing insight is that 'diversification is the only free lunch': finding about 15 uncorrelated return streams can sharply cut risk with almost no drop in expected return — he calls it the 'Holy Grail of investing.' On it he builds the 'All Weather' portfolio: rather than predict the future, make a portfolio that can't be wiped out in any quadrant — inflation/deflation, growth/recession — by balancing assets according to 'risk' rather than dollar amounts (risk parity).
The larger backdrop is the 'economic machine' and debt cycles. He sees the economy as an intelligible machine driven by long-term productivity growth layered with short- and long-term debt cycles; reading their swings explains booms, bubbles, deleveragings and depressions. In later years he scaled this cyclical view up to a 'changing world order' — the rise and fall of empires, the turnover of reserve currencies, and great-power rivalry.

assessments.text: 被列为全球最具影响力的人物之一；桥水在其带领下一度成为全球管理规模最大的对冲基金。
有人质疑桥水「极度透明」文化的实操与回报可复制性，也质疑「全天候」在某些利率/市场环境下的表现；其宏观「大周期」论亦被指过于宿命或简化。

assessments_en.text: Listed among the world's most influential people; under him Bridgewater became, for a time, the largest hedge fund by assets under management.

Some question how workable — and how replicable in returns — Bridgewater's 'radical transparency' culture really is, and how 'All Weather' fares in certain rate/market regimes; his macro 'big cycle' thesis is also criticized as overly deterministic or simplified.

quotes: 痛苦 + 反思 = 进步。
极度求真，极度透明。
分散，是投资里唯一的免费午餐。
与其预测未来，不如让自己在任何未来里都不被打垮。
quotes_en: Pain + Reflection = Progress.
Radical truth and radical transparency.
Diversification is the only free lunch in investing.
Rather than predict the future, make sure no future can wipe you out.
works: 《债务危机：我的应对原则》(Principles for Navigating Big Debt Crises)
《原则：应对变化中的世界秩序》(Principles for Dealing with the Changing World Order)
《经济机器是怎样运行的》(How the Economic Machine Works，30 分钟动画)
works_en: 'Principles for Dealing with the Changing World Order'
'How the Economic Machine Works' (a 30-minute animated explainer)
dalio.lineage: 投资上自成一派（全天候/风险平价），但承接现代投资组合理论「分散降险」的内核（马科维茨一脉），与凯恩斯式宏观、明斯基的「金融不稳定假说」相呼应；「原则」「极度透明」则带有斯多葛式的理性自律与系统工程色彩。影响了一批宏观与资产配置型投资者。
dalio.lineage_en: In investing he stands on his own (All Weather / risk parity) yet inherits the 'diversification cuts risk' core of modern portfolio theory (the Markowitz line) and echoes Keynesian macro and Minsky's 'financial instability hypothesis'; his 'principles' and 'radical transparency' carry a Stoic rationalism and a systems-engineering flavor. He has influenced a generation of macro and asset-allocation investors.
dalio.trivia: 1975 年在自家公寓白手起家创办桥水；《经济机器是怎样运行的》30 分钟动画在网上广为流传；2017 年《原则》成为全球畅销书；据他自述，年轻时曾因极度看空美国经济而严重误判、几乎赔光、不得不遣散团队并向父亲借钱——这段惨痛教训，反而促成了他对「分散」与「极度求真」的终身执念；约 2022 年完成桥水的领导权交接。
dalio.trivia_en: He founded Bridgewater from his apartment in 1975; his 30-minute animation 'How the Economic Machine Works' went widely viral; 'Principles' (2017) became a global bestseller; by his own account, a young Dalio made a catastrophic bet betting against the US economy, nearly went broke, had to let his team go and borrow from his father — a painful lesson that seeded his lifelong obsession with diversification and 'radical truth'; he completed Bridgewater's leadership transition around 2022.

maslow.bio: 亚伯拉罕·马斯洛，1908–1970，美国心理学家，人本主义心理学（被称为心理学『第三势力』，与精神分析、行为主义并列）的奠基者。他不满于当时心理学只盯着病人与本能，主张转而研究健康、成熟、富有创造力的人——去问『人最好能成为什么样子』。代表作《动机与人格》《存在心理学探索》。晚年提出超越个人的灵性需求。
maslow.bio_en: Abraham Maslow, 1908–1970, American psychologist and founder of humanistic psychology — the 'third force' alongside psychoanalysis and behaviorism. Dissatisfied that psychology fixed only on the sick and on instinct, he urged studying healthy, mature, creative people — asking 'what can a person at best become?' His major works are 'Motivation and Personality' and 'Toward a Psychology of Being.' Late in life he added a transpersonal, spiritual tier of need.
maslow.ideas:
马斯洛最广为人知的是『需求层次』：人的需要大致由低到高排成几层——生理（吃饱睡足）、安全、归属与爱、尊重，最顶端是『自我实现』，即成为你所能成为的那个人。低层需要被剥夺时会主宰一切，一旦稳定满足，注意力才会自然升到更高层。
他更深的一个区分是『缺失性动机』与『成长性（存在）动机』。缺失性动机出于匮乏——你做事是为了补上缺的安全、认可、爱；它像止痛，满足了就暂停。成长性动机出于充盈——你做事是因为活动本身让你舒展、创造、给予；它越满足越想要，不会饱和。同一件事，可以由这两种完全不同的根来驱动。
他还研究『高峰体验』：那些忘我、合一、时间消失的瞬间，常出现在自我实现者身上。
要紧的是：马斯洛并不否定低层需要——它们真实而必要；他只是指出，一个人若一辈子停在『用成就去补匮乏』，就永远走不到『从安稳里自然生长』的那一层。
maslow.ideas_en:
Maslow is best known for the 'hierarchy of needs': human needs roughly stack from low to high — physiological (food, sleep), safety, belonging and love, esteem, and at the top 'self-actualization,' becoming the person you are capable of being. When a lower need is starved it dominates everything; once it is steadily met, attention rises naturally to the higher tiers.
His deeper distinction is between 'deficiency motivation' and 'growth (being) motivation.' Deficiency motivation springs from lack — you act to fill missing safety, approval or love; like a painkiller, it pauses once satisfied. Growth motivation springs from fullness — you act because the activity itself lets you stretch, create, give; the more it is fed the more it wants, never saturating. The very same act can be driven by these two utterly different roots.
He also studied 'peak experiences' — self-losing, unitive, timeless moments common in self-actualizers.
Crucially, Maslow does not dismiss the lower needs — they are real and necessary; he only notes that someone who spends a whole life 'using achievement to patch a lack' never reaches the tier of 'growing naturally out of security.'

assessments.text: 被视为人本主义与积极心理学的先驱——把心理学的目光从病态转向健康与潜能。
需求层次的『严格逐级上升』缺乏充分实证支持，跨文化普适性也受质疑；但『缺失 vs 成长动机』的洞见仍广受认可。

assessments_en.text: Seen as a forerunner of humanistic and positive psychology — turning psychology's gaze from pathology toward health and potential.

The strict step-by-step ascent of the hierarchy lacks firm empirical support and its cross-cultural universality is questioned; yet the 'deficiency vs growth motivation' insight remains widely embraced.

quotes: 人能成为什么，他就必须成为什么。
满足了的需要不再是激励者。
若你只有一把锤子，就容易把一切都看成钉子。
quotes_en: What a man can be, he must be.
A satisfied need is no longer a motivator.
If the only tool you have is a hammer, you tend to see every problem as a nail.
works: 《存在心理学探索》(Toward a Psychology of Being)
maslow.lineage: 承接人本主义传统（与罗杰斯并称），反拨精神分析的病理取向与行为主义的机械论；下启塞利格曼、契克森米哈伊等积极心理学，也深刻影响了管理学（如自我实现型员工）。
maslow.lineage_en: Carries the humanistic tradition (paired with Carl Rogers), pushing back on psychoanalysis's pathology focus and behaviorism's mechanism; he in turn shaped positive psychology (Seligman, Csikszentmihalyi) and management thought (the self-actualizing employee).
maslow.trivia: 早年做灵长类与依恋研究；提出需求层次时并未画成那座著名的『金字塔』——金字塔图是后人加的；晚年在需求层次顶端之上又补了『超越性需求』(self-transcendence)，惜未及充分展开便去世。
maslow.trivia_en: He began in primate and attachment research; he never drew the famous 'pyramid' — that diagram was added by others; late in life he placed a tier of 'self-transcendence' above self-actualization, but died before fully developing it.

csikszentmihalyi.bio: 米哈里·契克森米哈伊，1934–2021，匈牙利裔美国心理学家，积极心理学的共同奠基者。他童年经历二战的动荡，毕生追问『人在什么时候最投入、最有幸福感』。他用『经验取样法』让上千人随身记录当下的状态，由此提炼出『心流』这一概念，代表作《心流：最优体验心理学》。
csikszentmihalyi.bio_en: Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi, 1934–2021, Hungarian-American psychologist and co-founder of positive psychology. Shaped by the upheavals of WWII in childhood, he spent his life asking 'when are people most absorbed and most fulfilled?' Using the 'experience sampling method,' he had thousands log their state in the moment, and from it distilled the concept of 'flow.' His major work is 'Flow: The Psychology of Optimal Experience.'
csikszentmihalyi.ideas:
契克森米哈伊的核心概念是『心流』：当一项活动的挑战难度与你的技能恰好匹配——不太难到焦虑，也不太易到无聊——你会进入一种全神贯注、忘我、时间感扭曲的状态。心流时，注意力高度有序，自我意识消失，行动与觉察合一；事后回想，那往往是人最充实、最接近幸福的时刻。
他由此提出『自带目的的活动』(autotelic)：为活动本身、而非为外部奖赏（钱、名、认可）去做的事。一个『自带目的的人』能从过程本身取得回报，因而内在动机充沛、不易被外部毁誉牵着走。
反面是『精神熵』：注意力被焦虑、担忧、杂念搅乱的失序状态。他认为幸福不是被动等来的，而是通过把注意力投入有挑战、有反馈、目标清晰的活动，主动『建构』出来的——心流可以训练，生活也可以被设计成更容易进入心流。
csikszentmihalyi.ideas_en:
Csikszentmihalyi's central concept is 'flow': when an activity's challenge matches your skill — not so hard it brings anxiety, not so easy it brings boredom — you enter a state of total absorption, self-forgetting, and distorted time. In flow, attention is highly ordered, self-consciousness vanishes, and action merges with awareness; looking back, these are often a person's fullest, happiest moments.
From this he draws the 'autotelic' activity: something done for its own sake rather than for an external reward (money, fame, approval). An 'autotelic person' draws reward from the process itself, so their intrinsic motivation runs deep and is not easily swayed by outside praise or blame.
Its opposite is 'psychic entropy': the disordered state in which attention is scrambled by anxiety, worry and distraction. He held that happiness is not passively awaited but actively 'built' by pouring attention into activities that are challenging, give feedback, and have clear goals — flow can be trained, and life can be designed to enter it more easily.

assessments.text: 与塞利格曼共同奠基积极心理学；『心流』成为心理学、教育、设计、体育与管理中被广泛援用的概念。
心流多依赖自我报告、难以客观测量；也有人指出过度追求心流可能美化『沉浸式劳动』、忽略其社会条件。

assessments_en.text: Co-founded positive psychology with Seligman; 'flow' became a widely used concept across psychology, education, design, sport and management.
Flow relies heavily on self-report and is hard to measure objectively; some note that over-valorizing flow can romanticize 'immersive work' and ignore its social conditions.

quotes: 人生最美好的时刻，往往发生在一个人为完成困难而值得的事、自愿把身心逼到极限的时候。
控制意识，就是控制体验的质量。
quotes_en: The best moments usually occur when a person's body or mind is stretched to its limits in a voluntary effort to accomplish something difficult and worthwhile.
To control consciousness is to control the quality of experience.
works: 《心流：最优体验心理学》(Flow: The Psychology of Optimal Experience)
csikszentmihalyi.lineage: 承接马斯洛的人本主义与『高峰体验』，把它操作化为可研究的『心流』；与塞利格曼并立为积极心理学两大支柱，影响教育、游戏设计、运动心理与组织管理。
csikszentmihalyi.lineage_en: Builds on Maslow's humanism and 'peak experiences,' operationalizing them into the researchable concept of 'flow'; stands with Seligman as a pillar of positive psychology, shaping education, game design, sport psychology and management.
csikszentmihalyi.trivia: 姓氏以难念著称（大致读作『契克森特米哈伊』），他本人也常自嘲；他发明的『经验取样法』——让被试随身佩戴呼叫器、随机响起时记录当下心境——是研究『日常幸福』的方法论突破。
csikszentmihalyi.trivia_en: His surname is famously hard to pronounce (roughly 'chick-sent-me-high'), and he often joked about it; his 'experience sampling method' — having subjects carry a pager and log their mood whenever it beeped — was a methodological breakthrough for studying everyday happiness.

kierkegaard.bio: 索伦·克尔凯郭尔（1813–1855），丹麦哲学家、神学家与作家，公认的存在主义先驱。生于哥本哈根一个虔敬而忧郁的富商家庭，一生几乎未离此城。他与未婚妻蕾琪娜的解除婚约、与丹麦教会及媒体的激烈论战，深刻塑造了他的写作。他常以众多化名出版著作，从不同人生立场发声，以『间接沟通』逼读者自己去抉择。四十二岁猝然病逝，身后其思想才被欧洲重新发现，影响深远。
kierkegaard.bio_en: Søren Kierkegaard (1813–1855) was a Danish philosopher, theologian, and writer, widely regarded as a forerunner of existentialism. Born in Copenhagen to a devout, melancholy, wealthy merchant family, he scarcely left the city his whole life. His broken engagement to Regine Olsen and his fierce polemics with the Danish church and press deeply shaped his writing. He often published under many pseudonyms, voicing different life-stances to force readers, through 'indirect communication,' to choose for themselves. He died suddenly at forty-two, and only afterward was his thought rediscovered by Europe, to lasting effect.
kierkegaard.ideas:
克尔凯郭尔毕生反对一种东西：把人生变成抽象的旁观。当时黑格尔的宏大体系试图把一切纳入理性的普遍进程，克尔凯郭尔反唇相讥：**再宏伟的体系也回答不了『我，此刻，该怎样活』这个唯一要紧的问题。真理不是一套你能站在外面观赏的客观命题，而是你必须亲身投入、以生命去担当的东西——『主观性即真理』。**

他描绘了人生的三个『阶段』或存在方式。审美阶段的人追逐新奇与享受，为逃避无聊而不断更换对象，却始终悬浮、不作承诺；伦理阶段的人开始认真选择、担起责任、忠于义务；宗教阶段的人则面对上帝、以『信仰之跃』纵身跳入理性无法担保的深渊。这三者不是知识的递进，而是一次次需要本人亲自抉择的跳跃。

他对现代人心理的洞察尤为惊人。他把『焦虑』定义为『自由的眩晕』：当人意识到自己面前有无限可能、且必须亲自选择时，会生出一种没有具体对象的晕眩不安——焦虑不是软弱，而是自由的证据。他又剖析『绝望』为『不肯成为真正的自己』的病症，可以安静到人浑然不觉。面对这一切，他的解药不是更多的知识或体系，而是勇气：敢于作为一个独一无二、会犯错、终将面对上帝与死亡的『单独个体』，去承担自己的存在。正是这份对个体、抉择、焦虑与本真的强调，使他成为二十世纪存在主义的源头。
kierkegaard.ideas_en:
Kierkegaard opposed one thing his whole life: turning existence into abstract spectatorship. As Hegel's grand system sought to fold everything into a universal march of reason, Kierkegaard shot back: **no system, however magnificent, can answer the one question that matters — 'how am I, here, now, to live.' Truth is not a set of objective propositions you can admire from outside, but something you must throw yourself into and carry with your life — 'subjectivity is truth.'**

He mapped three 'stages' or modes of existence. The aesthetic person chases novelty and enjoyment, forever swapping objects to flee boredom, yet stays suspended, committing to nothing; the ethical person begins to choose in earnest, take on responsibility, and stay faithful to duty; the religious person faces God and, in a 'leap of faith,' plunges into an abyss reason cannot secure. These are not steps of knowledge but leaps each person must make in their own act of choice.

His insight into the modern psyche is especially striking. He defines 'anxiety' as 'the dizziness of freedom': when a person realizes that infinite possibility lies before them and they must choose themselves, a vertiginous unease with no specific object arises — anxiety is not weakness but the evidence of freedom. He dissects 'despair' as the sickness of refusing to become one's true self, one so quiet a person may not notice it at all. Against all this his remedy is not more knowledge or system but courage: to dare, as a unique, fallible 'single individual' who will finally face God and death, to take up one's own existence. This very stress on the individual, choice, anxiety, and authenticity makes him the wellspring of twentieth-century existentialism.

assessments.text: 在《存在与时间》中承认克尔凯郭尔对『畏』（Angst）与个体生存的分析给予其深刻启发，尽管批评他仍停留于生存层面而未及存在论。
曾称克尔凯郭尔为十九世纪最深刻的思想家、一位圣徒，钦佩其对宗教与生存之诚实，虽自认无力追随其信仰之路。

assessments_en.text: In Being and Time he acknowledges that Kierkegaard's analysis of 'anxiety' (Angst) and individual existence gave him deep stimulus, even as he faults him for remaining at the existentiell level and not reaching ontology.

He called Kierkegaard the most profound thinker of the nineteenth century, 'a saint,' admiring his honesty about religion and existence, though he confessed himself unable to follow his path of faith.

quotes: 人生只能倒着被理解，却必须正着去活。
焦虑是自由的眩晕。
去冒险，会一时失去立足；不去冒险，却会失去自己。
最大的危险——失去自我——可以在世上悄然发生，仿佛什么都没有。
quotes_en: Life can only be understood backwards; but it must be lived forwards.
Anxiety is the dizziness of freedom.
To dare is to lose one's footing momentarily; not to dare is to lose oneself.
The greatest hazard of all, losing the self, can occur very quietly in the world, as if it were nothing at all.
kierkegaard.lineage: 以反黑格尔体系、返回个体生存为立场，上承奥古斯丁、帕斯卡尔的信仰内省传统；身后深刻影响海德格尔、雅斯贝尔斯、萨特、加缪等存在主义者，以及巴特的辩证神学，被公认为存在主义之父。
kierkegaard.lineage_en: Standing against Hegel's system and returning to individual existence, he inherited the tradition of faith and self-examination from Augustine and Pascal; after his death he profoundly shaped existentialists such as Heidegger, Jaspers, Sartre, and Camus, and Barth's dialectical theology, and is recognized as the father of existentialism.
kierkegaard.trivia: 他与蕾琪娜·奥尔森解除婚约一事，成为他一生的隐痛与创作母题——他似乎认定自己注定要为思想与信仰而牺牲世俗幸福，此后许多化名著作都在反复回应这场抉择留下的情感回响。
kierkegaard.trivia_en: His breaking of the engagement to Regine Olsen became the private wound and recurring motif of his life — he seemed convinced he was fated to sacrifice worldly happiness for thought and faith, and many of his later pseudonymous works keep answering the emotional echoes of that choice.

seneca.bio: 塞内卡（约前 4–公元 65），全名卢基乌斯·安奈乌斯·塞内卡，古罗马斯多葛派哲学家、政治家与悲剧作家，史称『小塞内卡』。生于西班牙科尔多瓦，在罗马研习修辞与哲学，历经流放与复起，一度任少年皇帝尼禄的老师与谋臣，权倾一时；晚年遭尼禄猜忌，被诬涉谋反而奉命自尽，从容赴死。传世有《道德书简》《论生命之短暂》《论愤怒》等散文，以及《美狄亚》等悲剧。
seneca.bio_en: Seneca (c. 4 BC – AD 65), in full Lucius Annaeus Seneca, was a Roman Stoic philosopher, statesman, and tragic dramatist, known as 'Seneca the Younger.' Born in Córdoba in Roman Spain, he trained in rhetoric and philosophy at Rome, endured exile and return, and for a time served as tutor and advisor to the young emperor Nero, wielding great power. Late in life, suspected by Nero and accused of conspiracy, he was ordered to take his own life and met death with composure. His surviving works include the Moral Letters, On the Shortness of Life, and On Anger, along with tragedies such as Medea.
seneca.ideas:
塞内卡的哲学是一种『生活的技艺』——他不追求体系的完备，而反复追问：一个人怎样才能活得好、死得安。作为斯多葛派，他坚持一个核心信念：**唯有德性是真正的善，其余（财富、地位、健康、名声）都是『无关紧要之物』**——它们本身不好也不坏，好坏只在你如何使用。因此外在的得失不该左右内心的安宁；能被夺走的，本就不是你真正拥有的。

他最打动后世的，是对时间与生命的思考。在《论生命之短暂》里他说：生命并不短，是我们把它浪费了——为他人而活、为琐事奔忙、把最重要的事一再推给将来，等到回头，才发现真正属于自己的时间所剩无几。与之配套的是他对死亡的态度：练习正视死亡，不是为了悲观，而是因为唯有意识到时日有限，人才会认真对待当下、分清什么值得。

他还是古代最细腻的『情绪治疗师』之一。《论愤怒》把愤怒剖析为一种可被理性识破、提前预防的冲动；他主张每晚自省（今天我克服了哪个弱点、哪里可以更好），把哲学当成日日操练的功夫，而非书斋里的学问。这种把大道理落到具体日常、写给普通人的笔调，让他的文字两千年后仍像一封贴心的来信。
seneca.ideas_en:
Seneca's philosophy is an 'art of living' — he sought not a complete system but kept asking one question: how does a person live well and die at peace. As a Stoic he held a core conviction: **virtue alone is the true good, while everything else — wealth, status, health, reputation — is 'indifferent,'** neither good nor bad in itself, its worth lying only in how you use it. So outward gains and losses should not sway inner calm; what can be taken from you was never truly yours.

What has moved posterity most is his thinking on time and life. In On the Shortness of Life he writes: life is not short, we waste it — living for others, busy with trifles, deferring what matters most to a future that shrinks until, looking back, we find little of our own time left. Paired with this is his stance on death: to practice facing it, not out of gloom, but because only awareness of a finite span makes a person take the present seriously and tell what is worth doing from what is not.

He is also one of antiquity's subtlest 'therapists of emotion.' On Anger dissects rage as an impulse that reason can see through and head off in advance; he urges a nightly self-examination — which weakness did I overcome today, where could I do better — treating philosophy as a daily exercise rather than book-learning. This habit of bringing lofty doctrine down to concrete daily life, in a voice addressed to ordinary people, keeps his prose reading, two thousand years on, like a letter from a close friend.

assessments.text: 在《编年史》中记述塞内卡奉命自尽的一幕：他从容与友人诀别、安慰哭泣的妻子，虽赴死而神色不乱，笔下透出对其风骨的敬重。
在《随笔集》中大量援引塞内卡，视之为切近生活的道德导师，称其文字如利刃，直入人心。

assessments_en.text: In the Annals he recounts Seneca's ordered suicide — calmly taking leave of friends, consoling his weeping wife, unshaken in the face of death — his account conveying respect for the man's fortitude.
His Essays quote Seneca abundantly, treating him as a moral teacher close to lived experience whose words cut like a blade straight to the heart.

quotes: 生命并不短，是我们浪费了太多。
我们受苦，常在想象中多于在现实中。
只要你还活着，就要继续学习如何生活。
每一天都当作完整的一生去安排。
quotes_en: It is not that we have a short time to live, but that we waste much of it.
We suffer more often in imagination than in reality.
As long as you live, keep learning how to live.
Arrange each day as if it were a complete life.
seneca.lineage: 上承芝诺、克律西波斯创立的斯多葛学派，与爱比克泰德、马可·奥勒留同为罗马斯多葛三大代表；其散文经中世纪教会与文艺复兴人文主义者传习，深刻影响蒙田、帕斯卡尔乃至近代的『生活哲学』传统。
seneca.lineage_en: He inherited the Stoic school founded by Zeno and Chrysippus and stands with Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius as one of the three great Roman Stoics; his prose, transmitted through the medieval church and Renaissance humanists, deeply shaped Montaigne, Pascal, and the modern tradition of 'philosophy as a way of life.'
seneca.trivia: 他既是宣讲清心寡欲的哲人，又是罗马巨富，还担任过尼禄的重臣——这种言行之间的张力，古今争议不断；他本人在书信里坦承自己远非圣贤，只是一个在途中、努力向善的病人，正因如此更显真诚。
seneca.trivia_en: He was at once a philosopher preaching simplicity, one of Rome's wealthiest men, and a chief minister to Nero — a tension between word and life that has drawn debate ever since; yet in his letters he freely admits he is no sage, only a patient still on the road, striving toward the good, which makes him all the more candid.

descartes.bio: 1596–1650，法国哲学家、数学家、科学家，被誉为近代哲学之父。生于法国图赖讷拉海，自幼体弱，在耶稣会拉弗莱什公学受良好教育。成年后长期旅居相对宽容的荷兰，潜心著述二十余年。他发明解析几何（今天的「笛卡尔坐标系」即以他命名），在光学、生理学上亦有贡献。1649 年应瑞典女王克里斯蒂娜之邀赴斯德哥尔摩讲学，因严寒与清晨授课染上肺炎，次年初病逝。
descartes.bio_en: 1596–1650, French philosopher, mathematician, and scientist, widely called the father of modern philosophy. Born at La Haye in Touraine and frail from childhood, he received an excellent education at the Jesuit college of La Flèche. As an adult he lived for more than twenty years in the relatively tolerant Dutch Republic, devoting himself to his writing. He invented analytic geometry (the "Cartesian coordinate system" bears his name) and made contributions to optics and physiology. In 1649 he accepted Queen Christina's invitation to teach in Stockholm; the harsh cold and early-morning lessons brought on pneumonia, and he died early the next year.
descartes.ideas:
笛卡尔想为一切知识找到一块绝对牢靠的地基。他生活的年代，旧的权威（教会、亚里士多德、古书）正在崩塌，新的科学刚刚兴起，到处是相互矛盾的说法。他问自己：有没有什么是我可以绝对确定、无论如何都怀疑不掉的？
他的办法叫「普遍怀疑」：把一切可疑的东西统统先当成假的剔除掉。感官会骗人（筷子插进水里看着是弯的），所以感官经验不可靠；做梦时也以为一切真实，所以连「我现在醒着」都不能保证；他甚至设想，会不会有一个「狡猾的恶魔」一直在欺骗我，让二加二在我看来等于四其实是错的？这样一路怀疑下去，几乎什么都站不住。但就在这里，他找到了那个怀疑不掉的支点：哪怕恶魔骗我，「我正在被骗、正在怀疑、正在思考」这件事本身总得是真的——因为如果我不存在，就没有「我」可被欺骗。于是有了那句不朽的话：**「我思故我在」(Cogito ergo sum)**。我可以怀疑一切，唯独不能怀疑「正在怀疑的我」存在。
以这个支点为起点，他重建知识：凡是像「我思故我在」一样「清晰而明白」地呈现在理性面前的观念，就可以当作真理。数学正是这种清晰明白的典范——这也是为什么他把数学当作一切可靠知识的模型。
他还提出了著名的「心物二元论」：世界由两种截然不同的东西组成。一种是「思维的实体」(res cogitans)，即心灵——它会思考、没有广延、不占空间；另一种是「广延的实体」(res extensa)，即物质——它占据空间、像机器一样按力学规律运转，包括我们的身体。在他看来，人的身体也是一台精巧的机器，只有心灵是非物质的。这一刀切下去，好处是：既然物质世界纯是机械，科学家就可以用数学和力学去精确解剖它，不必再问它有什么「目的」或「灵魂」——近代自然科学正是踩着这块跳板起飞的。但这一刀也留下了一个折磨了哲学几百年的难题：如果心灵和身体是两种毫不相干的东西，它们到底怎么互相作用？我一「想」抬手，手就抬了，这是怎么发生的？这就是著名的「身心问题」。
无论后人如何批评，笛卡尔做了一件划时代的事：他把确定性的根基，从外在的权威与传统，搬到了每一个人自己「会思考的我」身上。从此，「我自己用理性去判断」成了现代人的基本姿态。
descartes.ideas_en:
Descartes wanted to find an absolutely secure foundation for all knowledge. He lived in an age when the old authorities—the Church, Aristotle, the ancient books—were crumbling and a new science was just being born, leaving contradictory claims everywhere. So he asked himself: is there anything I can be absolutely certain of, anything I cannot doubt no matter what?
His method was "methodic doubt": provisionally treat as false everything that can be doubted at all. The senses deceive us (a stick looks bent in water), so sense experience is unreliable; in dreams everything seems real, so I cannot even be sure "I am now awake"; he even imagined an "evil demon" forever deceiving me, making two plus two look like four when it is really wrong. Doubting all the way down, almost nothing survives. But just here he found the one indubitable point: even if a demon deceives me, the very fact that "I am being deceived, am doubting, am thinking" must be true—for if I did not exist, there would be no "I" to deceive. Hence the immortal line: **"I think, therefore I am" (Cogito ergo sum).** I can doubt everything except that the doubting "I" exists.
From this fulcrum he rebuilt knowledge: whatever presents itself to reason as "clearly and distinctly" as the cogito may be taken as true. Mathematics is the very model of such clear-and-distinct knowing—which is why he made it the model for all reliable knowledge.
He also proposed his famous "mind-body dualism": the world is made of two utterly different kinds of thing. One is "thinking substance" (res cogitans), the mind—it thinks, has no extension, occupies no space; the other is "extended substance" (res extensa), matter—which fills space and runs by mechanical laws like a machine, including our bodies. For him the human body too is an exquisite machine; only the mind is immaterial. The benefit of this cut: since the material world is purely mechanical, scientists can dissect it precisely with mathematics and mechanics, no longer asking what "purpose" or "soul" it has—and modern natural science took off from exactly this springboard. But the cut also left a problem that tormented philosophy for centuries: if mind and body are two wholly unrelated things, how do they interact at all? I merely "will" to raise my arm and it rises—how does that happen? This is the famous "mind-body problem."
Whatever his critics say, Descartes did something epoch-making: he moved the ground of certainty from external authority and tradition onto each person's own "thinking I." Ever since, "judging for myself with my own reason" has been the basic posture of the modern person.

assessments.text: 在《哲学史讲演录》中盛赞笛卡尔重新开创了哲学，说哲学到了他这里「就像航海者在长久漂泊后终于望见陆地」，从此进入一个全新的时代（大意）。
神经科学家达马西奥以《笛卡尔的错误》为题，指他把理性与情感、心灵与身体强行劈开是一个根本失误——现代脑科学表明，情绪恰恰是理性决策不可或缺的基础。

assessments_en.text: In his Lectures on the History of Philosophy, Hegel hailed Descartes as having begun philosophy anew, saying that with him philosophy is "like a mariner who, after a long voyage on stormy seas, at last sights land"—the entry into a wholly new age (paraphrased).

The neuroscientist Antonio Damasio titled a book Descartes' Error, arguing that cleaving reason from emotion and mind from body was a fundamental mistake—modern brain science shows emotion is in fact indispensable to rational decision-making.

quotes: 我思故我在。（Cogito, ergo sum.）
良知（理性）是世界上分配得最公平的东西——人人都觉得自己已经够用，不想要更多。（《谈谈方法》开篇，大意）
读一本好书，就是在与过去几个世纪里最杰出的人交谈。（《谈谈方法》，大意）
quotes_en: I think, therefore I am. (Cogito, ergo sum.)
Good sense is the most fairly distributed thing in the world—everyone thinks he is so well supplied with it that he wants no more. (Discourse on the Method, opening; paraphrased)
The reading of all good books is like a conversation with the finest minds of past centuries. (Discourse on the Method; paraphrased)
works: 《谈谈方法》(1637，附《几何学》提出解析几何)
works_en: Discourse on the Method (1637, with the appended Geometry that founded analytic geometry)
descartes.lineage: 近代理性论的开端，直接影响斯宾诺莎、莱布尼茨；与经验论的培根、洛克分庭抗礼，二者的张力催生了康德的综合。其心物二元留下的「身心问题」，至今仍是心灵哲学与认知科学的核心议题。
descartes.lineage_en: The starting point of modern rationalism, directly shaping Spinoza and Leibniz; set against the empiricism of Bacon and Locke, a tension that later drove Kant's synthesis. The "mind-body problem" his dualism left behind remains a central question in philosophy of mind and cognitive science.
descartes.trivia: 据传他习惯晚起、常在床上沉思，解析几何中用坐标定位点的灵感，传说来自躺着看天花板上爬动的苍蝇（轶事，未必可考）；他一生谨慎，因伽利略受审而推迟出版《论世界》；身后遗骨几经辗转，头骨与躯体一度分离。
descartes.trivia_en: He was said to rise late and meditate in bed; legend has it that the idea of locating points by coordinates came from watching a fly crawl across his ceiling (an anecdote of doubtful authority). Cautious by temperament, he withheld his treatise The World after Galileo's trial; after his death his remains were moved repeatedly, and his skull was for a time separated from his body.

hegel.bio: 1770–1831，德国哲学家，德国唯心论的集大成者。生于斯图加特，青年时在图宾根神学院与荷尔德林、谢林同窗。先后任教于耶拿、海德堡，最终成为柏林大学哲学讲席教授、当时德意志思想界的中心人物。其体系宏大艰深，几乎笼罩了之后一个世纪的哲学、政治与历史思考。1831 年死于柏林的霍乱流行。
hegel.bio_en: 1770–1831, German philosopher and the culminating figure of German idealism. Born in Stuttgart, he studied at the Tübingen seminary alongside Hölderlin and Schelling. He taught at Jena and Heidelberg before becoming professor of philosophy at the University of Berlin, the central figure of German intellectual life of his day. His vast and difficult system would dominate philosophical, political, and historical thought for the next century. He died in Berlin's cholera epidemic of 1831.
hegel.ideas:
黑格尔最核心的洞见是：真理不是一个静止的结论，而是一个运动的过程。万事万物——从一个概念、一段历史，到整个宇宙——都在不断地自我发展、自我超越。
推动这个过程的引擎，就是他著名的「辩证法」。简单说：任何一个立场（正题）内部都藏着自己的对立面（反题），二者冲突、撕扯，最后被一个更高的立场（合题）所「扬弃」。「扬弃」(Aufhebung)是个绝妙的德文词，一身三义：既「否定」掉旧的，又「保留」其合理内核，还把它「提升」到更高层次——就像孩子长成大人，并非简单抹掉童年，而是把它收纳进更成熟的自己里。重要的是：那个「合题」往往又成了新的「正题」，引出新一轮对立与超越。所以历史和思想不是原地打转，而是螺旋式地向前、向上。
他用这套眼光看历史，提出了一个大胆的判断：整部人类史，是「绝对精神」(Geist，也译『绝对理念』)逐步认识自己、实现自由的过程。这里的「精神」不是某个神，而更像贯穿历史的理性本身。它通过一个个民族、一场场冲突、甚至无数个体的私欲与野心，曲折地把「自由」一步步变成现实——他称这种「让人的私利在不知不觉中成就更大历史目的」的机制为「理性的狡计」。他由此得出那句最常被引用、也最常被误解的话：「凡是合理的都是现实的，凡是现实的都是合理的」——意思并非「现状都对」，而是说现实背后有理性的脉络可循。
在《精神现象学》里，他讲了一个影响深远的故事——「主奴辩证法」：两个自我意识相遇，为求对方承认而殊死相争，败者为保命而臣服为奴、胜者为主。但吊诡的是，主人渐渐依赖奴隶的劳动而变得空虚，奴隶却在改造世界的劳动中获得了真实的自我与成长——主奴关系于是悄悄翻转。这个关于「承认」与「劳动」的故事，后来深深启发了马克思和整个左翼思想。
黑格尔的野心是把一切对立——主观与客观、个体与社会、自由与必然——都收摄进一个不断生长的整体之中。他有句名言：「真理是全体」。理解任何片段，都要看它在那个更大的、运动着的整体里处于什么位置。
hegel.ideas_en:
Hegel's central insight is that truth is not a fixed conclusion but a moving process. Everything—a concept, a stretch of history, the whole cosmos—is constantly developing and surpassing itself.
The engine of this process is his famous "dialectic." Put simply: any position (thesis) contains its own opposite within it (antithesis); the two clash and strain, and are finally "sublated" into a higher position (synthesis). "Sublation" (Aufhebung) is a marvelous German word with three senses at once—it negates the old, preserves its rational core, and lifts it to a higher level, the way a child becoming an adult does not simply erase childhood but takes it up into a more mature self. Crucially, that synthesis often becomes a new thesis, provoking a fresh round of opposition and transcendence. So history and thought do not spin in place but advance in an upward spiral.
Applying this lens to history, he made a bold claim: the whole of human history is the process by which "Spirit" (Geist, also "the Absolute Idea") gradually comes to know itself and realize freedom. "Spirit" here is not some god but more like reason itself running through history. Through one nation after another, one conflict after another, even through countless individual passions and ambitions, it turns "freedom" step by crooked step into reality—he called this mechanism, by which private interests unwittingly serve a larger historical end, the "cunning of reason." Hence his most-quoted and most-misread line: "What is rational is actual, and what is actual is rational"—meaning not "whatever exists is right," but that there is a traceable rational thread behind reality.
In the Phenomenology of Spirit he told a deeply influential story—the "master-slave dialectic." Two self-consciousnesses meet and fight to the death for recognition; the loser submits as slave to save his life, the winner becomes master. But paradoxically the master grows hollow, dependent on the slave's labor, while the slave, through the labor of transforming the world, gains a real self and grows—so the relation quietly reverses. This story of "recognition" and "labor" later deeply inspired Marx and the whole of left-wing thought.
Hegel's ambition was to gather every opposition—subject and object, individual and society, freedom and necessity—into a single, ever-growing whole. As he put it, "the truth is the whole." To understand any fragment, you must see where it stands within that larger, moving totality.

assessments.text: 马克思自承是黑格尔的学生，却说在黑格尔那里辩证法「倒立着」，必须把它「翻转过来、重新用脚站立」，才能从思辨的唯心论中救出其合理内核（《资本论》第二版跋，大意）。
同代论敌叔本华对他极尽嘲讽，斥之为故弄玄虚的「江湖骗子」，认为其晦涩文风败坏了德国哲学（大意）——这场敌意更多是文人相轻，却也代表了一种长存的批评。

assessments_en.text: Marx called himself Hegel's pupil yet said the dialectic stood "on its head" in Hegel and had to be "turned right side up" to recover its rational kernel from speculative idealism (afterword to the second edition of Capital, paraphrased).

His contemporary rival Schopenhauer heaped scorn on him as a mystifying "charlatan" whose obscure style corrupted German philosophy (paraphrased)—venom that was partly professional jealousy, yet voices a lasting line of criticism.

quotes: 凡是合理的都是现实的，凡是现实的都是合理的。（《法哲学原理》序言）
密涅瓦的猫头鹰要等黄昏到来，才会起飞。（《法哲学原理》序言；意指哲学总是事后才理解一个时代）
我们从历史中学到的唯一教训，就是人们从不从历史中汲取教训。（常被引述，大意）
quotes_en: What is rational is actual, and what is actual is rational. (Preface to the Philosophy of Right)
The owl of Minerva spreads its wings only with the falling of dusk. (Preface to the Philosophy of Right; philosophy understands an age only in hindsight)
The only thing we learn from history is that we learn nothing from history. (widely attributed; paraphrased)
works: 身后由学生整理的《历史哲学讲演录》《美学讲演录》《哲学史讲演录》
works_en: Elements of the Philosophy of Right (1820)
Posthumous lecture series on the philosophy of history, aesthetics, and the history of philosophy
hegel.lineage: 上承康德、费希特、谢林，集德国唯心论之大成。其身后门徒分裂为「老年黑格尔派」与激进的「青年（左派）黑格尔派」，后者经费尔巴哈通向马克思。其辩证法与历史哲学深刻塑造了马克思主义、存在主义与 20 世纪的科耶夫、法兰克福学派。
hegel.lineage_en: Building on Kant, Fichte, and Schelling, he brought German idealism to its summit. After his death his followers split into "Right" and radical "Young (Left) Hegelians," the latter passing through Feuerbach to Marx. His dialectic and philosophy of history profoundly shaped Marxism, existentialism, and twentieth-century thinkers from Kojève to the Frankfurt School.
hegel.trivia: 图宾根神学院时期与荷尔德林、谢林同住一室，三人共栽一棵「自由之树」以庆祝法国大革命；据说他在耶拿战役、拿破仑率军入城前夜赶完《精神现象学》，并称在街上望见马背上的拿破仑，是「看见了骑在马背上的世界精神」（大意）。
hegel.trivia_en: At the Tübingen seminary he shared a room with Hölderlin and Schelling, and the three planted a "tree of liberty" to celebrate the French Revolution; he is said to have finished the Phenomenology on the eve of the Battle of Jena as Napoleon's army entered the town, remarking that he had seen, in Napoleon riding through the streets, "the world-soul on horseback" (paraphrased).

russell.bio: 1872–1970，英国哲学家、数理逻辑学家、社会评论家与和平主义者，分析哲学的奠基人之一。出身英国贵族世家（祖父曾两任首相），幼年父母双亡，由祖母抚养。在剑桥三一学院研究数学与哲学，与怀特海合著《数学原理》。一生著述与社会活动并行：因反战两度入狱、晚年领导反核运动，1950 年获诺贝尔文学奖。享年 97 岁。
russell.bio_en: 1872–1970, British philosopher, mathematical logician, social critic, and pacifist, and one of the founders of analytic philosophy. Born into the British aristocracy (his grandfather was twice prime minister) and orphaned young, he was raised by his grandmother. At Trinity College, Cambridge he pursued mathematics and philosophy, co-authoring Principia Mathematica with Whitehead. His life ran along two tracks at once, writing and activism: he was jailed twice for opposing war, led the anti-nuclear movement in old age, and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1950. He lived to 97.
russell.ideas:
罗素相信哲学的首要美德是「清晰」，首要敌人是「含糊与教条」。他毕生都在做一件事：把含混的大问题，拆解成可以一块块清楚处理的小问题。
他最硬核的贡献在逻辑与数学。他与怀特海合写的《数学原理》，试图证明整个数学都能从纯逻辑推导出来（这叫「逻辑主义」）——为此他们从最基本的逻辑公理出发，足足推了几百页才证明「1+1=2」。途中他还发现了著名的「罗素悖论」：设想「所有不包含自身的集合」组成的集合，它到底包不包含自身？包含则矛盾，不包含也矛盾——这个悖论动摇了数学的地基，逼出了整个 20 世纪对逻辑基础的反思。
在哲学方法上，他提出「摹状词理论」，被誉为分析哲学的范本。比如「当今的法国国王是秃头」这句话——法国根本没有国王，那这句话是真是假？罗素的妙招是：把它「翻译」成几条清楚的逻辑断言（存在一个 x，x 是当今法国国王，且 x 是秃头……），一翻译，假象就破了——它只是个假命题，并不需要假设有个「不存在的国王」幽灵般地存在。他借此示范：许多哲学难题其实是被语言的表面语法骗出来的，把语言分析清楚，问题就消解了。这种「逻辑分析」的精神，定义了此后整个英美分析哲学。
但罗素绝不只是书斋里的逻辑学家。他是 20 世纪最著名的公共知识分子之一，毕生为自由思想、和平与理性辩护，反对一切教条——无论宗教的还是政治的。他写《我为什么不是基督徒》，也写《幸福之路》教普通人如何减少焦虑、活得通达。他的怀疑主义不是犬儒，而是一种谦逊：既然我可能是错的，就该容忍异见、跟着证据走。他在自传开篇说，支配自己一生的是三种激情：对爱的渴望、对知识的追求，以及对人类苦难「不可遏制的同情」。逻辑的冷峻与人道的热忱，在他身上奇妙地合一。
russell.ideas_en:
Russell believed the first virtue of philosophy is clarity and its first enemy is vagueness and dogma. His lifelong project was to break large, muddy questions into small ones that can be handled cleanly, one piece at a time.
His hardest-core contribution lay in logic and mathematics. Principia Mathematica, written with Whitehead, tried to show that the whole of mathematics could be derived from pure logic ("logicism")—starting from the most basic logical axioms, they needed hundreds of pages just to prove that "1+1=2." Along the way he discovered the famous "Russell's paradox": consider the set of all sets that do not contain themselves—does it contain itself? If it does, contradiction; if it doesn't, contradiction too. The paradox shook the foundations of mathematics and forced a century of reflection on the basis of logic.
In method he offered the "theory of descriptions," hailed as a paradigm of analytic philosophy. Take "the present King of France is bald"—France has no king, so is the sentence true or false? Russell's trick was to "translate" it into a few clear logical claims (there exists an x such that x is the present King of France, and x is bald...). Once translated, the illusion dissolves: it is simply a false statement, with no need to posit a ghostly "nonexistent king" who somehow exists. He thus showed that many philosophical puzzles are conjured by the surface grammar of language; analyze the language clearly and the puzzle disappears. This spirit of "logical analysis" defined Anglo-American analytic philosophy ever after.
Yet Russell was never merely a study-bound logician. He was one of the most famous public intellectuals of the twentieth century, defending free thought, peace, and reason all his life, opposing every dogma—religious or political. He wrote Why I Am Not a Christian, but also The Conquest of Happiness, teaching ordinary people how to lessen anxiety and live with poise. His skepticism was not cynicism but humility: since I might be wrong, I should tolerate dissent and follow the evidence. In the prologue to his autobiography he said three passions governed his life: the longing for love, the search for knowledge, and "unbearable pity for the suffering of mankind." The coldness of logic and the warmth of humanity fused strangely in him.

assessments.text: 1950 年授予他诺贝尔文学奖，表彰他「多样而重要的著作，持续捍卫人道主义理想与思想自由」。
其学生维特根斯坦早年深受其逻辑工作影响，后来与他在哲学方向上分道扬镳；二人复杂的师生关系本身，即是 20 世纪哲学的一段重要篇章。

assessments_en.text: Awarding him the 1950 Nobel Prize in Literature "in recognition of his varied and significant writings in which he champions humanitarian ideals and freedom of thought."

His student Wittgenstein was deeply shaped by his early logical work before diverging from him philosophically; their complex teacher-pupil relationship is itself an important chapter in twentieth-century philosophy.

quotes: 我绝不会为我的信念去死，因为我可能是错的。（广为流传，大意）
这世界的麻烦在于：愚人和狂热者总是无比笃定，而智者满腹狐疑。（大意）
对爱的渴望、对知识的追求、对人类苦难不可遏制的同情——这三种纯粹而无比强烈的激情，支配了我的一生。（《罗素自传》序言）
quotes_en: I would never die for my beliefs, because I might be wrong. (widely attributed; paraphrased)
The trouble with the world is that the stupid are cocksure while the intelligent are full of doubt. (paraphrased)

Three passions, simple but overwhelmingly strong, have governed my life: the longing for love, the search for knowledge, and unbearable pity for the suffering of mankind. (prologue to his Autobiography)
works_en: Our Knowledge of the External World (1914)
Why I Am Not a Christian (1927)
russell.lineage: 与弗雷格、摩尔同为分析哲学的奠基者，是维特根斯坦的老师，深刻影响了维也纳学派的逻辑实证主义与整个英美分析传统。作为公共知识分子，他也接续了密尔以降的英国自由主义与和平主义脉络。
russell.lineage_en: With Frege and Moore a founder of analytic philosophy, teacher of Wittgenstein, he deeply influenced the logical positivism of the Vienna Circle and the whole Anglo-American analytic tradition. As a public intellectual he also carried forward the British liberal and pacifist line descending from Mill.
russell.trivia: 一战期间因公开反战被罚款、剥夺三一学院教职，并一度入狱，在狱中仍埋头写哲学；1920 年曾访问中国并讲学近一年，写下《中国问题》；1955 年与爱因斯坦联名发表反核的《罗素—爱因斯坦宣言》；九十多岁仍上街反对越战。
russell.trivia_en: During the First World War he was fined, stripped of his Trinity lectureship for openly opposing the war, and briefly imprisoned—where he kept writing philosophy; in 1920 he visited China and lectured there for nearly a year, producing The Problem of China; in 1955 he issued the anti-nuclear Russell–Einstein Manifesto with Einstein; and in his nineties he still took to the streets against the Vietnam War.

shankara.bio: 约 8 世纪，南印度喀拉拉地区人，印度「不二吠檀多」(Advaita Vedanta)哲学的集大成者。相传他英年早逝（约 32 岁），却在短暂一生中遍游印度，与佛教及各派学者反复论辩，重振了婆罗门正统，并在印度东南西北创立四大修院（maṭha），其僧团传统延续至今。他为《梵经》《奥义书》《薄伽梵歌》所作的注释，成为印度哲学的奠基文献。
shankara.bio_en: Around the 8th century, born in the Kerala region of South India, Shankara was the great systematizer of "Advaita Vedanta," the non-dualist school of Indian philosophy. Tradition holds that he died young (about 32) yet in his brief life traveled across India, debating Buddhists and rival schools and reviving Brahmanical orthodoxy, founding four great monasteries (maṭhas) in the country's four corners whose monastic lineages survive to this day. His commentaries on the Brahma Sutras, the Upanishads, and the Bhagavad Gita became foundational texts of Indian thought.
shankara.ideas:
商羯罗要回答一个终极问题：什么才是真正、绝对真实的？他的答案石破天惊——只有一个东西真实，那就是「梵」(Brahman)：无形、无限、永恒、不可言说的纯粹意识，是万有的唯一根基。
他最惊人的主张，浓缩为一句「梵我一如」：你内心最深处那个「我」(Atman，真我)，与宇宙的终极实在「梵」，本质上是同一个东西，毫无二致。古老的奥义书有一句箴言「Tat tvam asi」（汝即彼，「那」就是你），商羯罗倾力阐发的正是它。注意：这个「真我」不是你的性格、身体、记忆或念头——那些都在生灭变化；它指的是那个始终在「观看」这一切的、纯粹的觉知本身。
那么，我们眼前这个五光十色、你我分明、生死流转的世界算什么？商羯罗说，它是「摩耶」(maya)——一种幻相，源于「无明」(avidya，根本的无知)。他有个著名的比喻：黄昏时你把地上的一根绳子错看成一条蛇，吓得魂飞魄散——蛇是真的吗？在你的体验里它千真万确，可一旦点灯看清，蛇当下消失，从来只有绳子。同理，把多样的世界、把一个个孤立的「小我」当成终极实在，就像把绳子看成蛇；一旦智慧之光亮起，看破的人就证悟到：从来只有「梵」这一个实在。另一个比喻是泥与陶罐：千万只形状各异的陶罐，本质无非是同一团泥——「梵」就是那团泥，万物只是它的不同形相。
所以他主张的解脱之道，不是靠行善积德、苦修或仪式（那些只在「世俗」层面有意义），而是靠「智慧」(jnana)——靠直接的洞见，亲证「我即是梵」，从无明的大梦中醒来。为帮人破除一切错误的指认，他常用「neti neti」（非此，非彼）的方法：梵不是身体，不是感官，不是心念……层层剥除一切「不是它」的东西，剩下那不可被剥除、不可被对象化的纯粹觉知，即是。
商羯罗还区分了「两重真理」：在「世俗的真实」里，世界、神明、道德、你我都照常运作，该尽的本分一样要尽；但在「最高的真实」里，唯有不二的梵。这一区分让他既能安顿日常生活，又坚守终极的一元论。他的思想是印度教哲学的高峰，也通过近代的辨喜等人，深刻影响了世界对印度精神的理解。
shankara.ideas_en:
Shankara set out to answer an ultimate question: what is truly, absolutely real? His answer is startling—only one thing is real, "Brahman": formless, infinite, eternal, ineffable pure consciousness, the sole ground of all that is.
His most astonishing claim is compressed into the phrase "Brahman and the self are one": that "I" in your innermost depth (Atman, the true Self) and the ultimate reality of the cosmos (Brahman) are in essence one and the same, without the slightest difference. The ancient Upanishadic dictum "Tat tvam asi" ("That thou art"—That is you) is precisely what Shankara devoted himself to expounding. Note: this "true Self" is not your personality, body, memories, or thoughts—all of which arise and pass; it is the pure awareness that is forever "witnessing" all of that.
Then what of this vivid world before us, with its sharp lines between you and me and its cycle of birth and death? Shankara says it is "maya"—an appearance, born of "avidya" (root ignorance). He offers a famous image: at dusk you mistake a rope on the ground for a snake and your soul leaps in terror—is the snake real? In your experience it is utterly real, yet the moment you bring a lamp and see clearly, the snake vanishes; there was only ever a rope. Likewise, taking the manifold world and each isolated "little self" as ultimately real is like seeing a snake in a rope; once the light of wisdom dawns, the one who sees through it realizes there was only ever the one reality, Brahman. Another image is clay and pots: ten thousand pots of every shape are essentially one lump of clay—Brahman is that clay, and all things are merely its forms.
So the liberation he teaches comes not through good deeds, austerity, or ritual (which matter only on the "worldly" level) but through "jnana," knowledge—through direct insight that realizes "I am Brahman," waking from the long dream of ignorance. To strip away every false identification he often used the method of "neti neti" ("not this, not that"): Brahman is not the body, not the senses, not the mind... peel away layer by layer everything that "is not it," and what remains—the pure awareness that cannot be peeled away or made an object—is it.
Shankara also distinguished "two levels of truth": on the level of "worldly reality," the world, the gods, morality, and you and I all function as usual, and the duties you owe must still be discharged; but on the level of "the highest reality," there is only non-dual Brahman. This distinction let him both honor daily life and hold fast to ultimate monism. His thought is a summit of Hindu philosophy and, through modern figures like Vivekananda, profoundly shaped the world's understanding of the Indian spirit.

assessments.text: 近代印度教改革家辨喜(Vivekananda)极为推崇商羯罗，将不二吠檀多视为印度精神的最高表达，并把它传向西方世界。
德国梵学家、叔本华的友人多伊森(Paul Deussen)盛赞不二吠檀多，认为它与柏拉图、康德的洞见遥相呼应，是人类思想的伟大成就之一（大意）。

assessments_en.text: The modern Hindu reformer Vivekananda revered Shankara, regarding Advaita Vedanta as the highest expression of the Indian spirit and carrying it to the Western world.
The German Indologist Paul Deussen, a friend of Schopenhauer, praised Advaita Vedanta as echoing the insights of Plato and Kant and as one of the great achievements of human thought (paraphrased).

quotes: 梵是真实，世界是幻；个体之我与梵不二，别无其他。（传为商羯罗，概括其纲领，大意）
Tat tvam asi——那，就是你。（出自《歌者奥义书》，商羯罗倾力阐发的核心箴言）
非此，非彼（neti neti）：凡可被指认者皆非真我。（其遮诠方法，大意）
quotes_en: Brahman is real, the world is illusion; the individual self is none other than Brahman. (attributed to Shankara as a summary of his program; paraphrased)
Tat tvam asi—That thou art. (from the Chandogya Upanishad; the core dictum Shankara devoted himself to expounding)
Not this, not that (neti neti): whatever can be pointed to is not the true Self. (his method of negation; paraphrased)
works: 对《歌者》《广林》等十部奥义书的注释
传为其作的《示教千则》(Upadeśasāhasrī)与《分辨宝鬘》(Vivekachudamani)
works_en: Commentaries on ten principal Upanishads (the Chandogya, Brihadaranyaka, and others)
Also attributed to him: the Upadeśasāhasrī and the Vivekachudamani
shankara.lineage: 上承《奥义书》与其师承乔荼波陀(Gaudapada)，将不二论系统化为吠檀多主流。后世罗摩奴阇(限定不二论)、摩陀婆(二元论)起而修正或反对他，形成吠檀多三大派的长久对峙。近代经辨喜等人，其影响远播欧美。
shankara.lineage_en: Building on the Upanishads and his teacher's teacher Gaudapada, he systematized non-dualism into the mainstream of Vedanta. Later Ramanuja (qualified non-dualism) and Madhva (dualism) arose to revise or oppose him, forming the long-standing rivalry of Vedanta's three great schools. Through Vivekananda and others his influence spread to Europe and America in the modern era.
shankara.trivia: 传说他 32 岁即英年早逝，却成就惊人；在印度东南西北创立的四大修院至今仍是印度教重镇；流传着许多论辩传奇，包括为辩赢对手之妻关于世俗生活的诘问，他「以神通暂离己身、附入一位刚死去的国王体内」去体验世情（传说）。
shankara.trivia_en: Legend says he died at just 32 yet achieved astonishingly much; the four monasteries he founded in India's four corners remain major Hindu centers today; many debate-legends surround him, including one in which, to win an argument with an opponent's wife about worldly life, he "left his own body by yogic power and entered the body of a just-deceased king" to taste worldly experience (a legend).

luxun.bio: 1881–1936，本名周树人，浙江绍兴人，中国现代文学的奠基者。早年留学日本仙台学医，因在课堂幻灯片中见到麻木围观同胞被杀的中国人，深受刺激，遂弃医从文，立志以文学疗救国民的精神。1918 年以「鲁迅」笔名发表《狂人日记》——中国第一篇现代白话短篇小说。此后以小说与杂文为武器，毕生解剖旧礼教与「国民劣根性」。
luxun.bio_en: 1881–1936, born Zhou Shuren in Shaoxing, Zhejiang, Lu Xun was the founder of modern Chinese literature. As a young man he studied medicine in Sendai, Japan; deeply shaken by a lantern-slide showing apathetic Chinese onlookers watching a fellow countryman being executed, he abandoned medicine for writing, resolved to heal his people's spirit through literature. In 1918, under the pen name "Lu Xun," he published "A Madman's Diary"—the first modern vernacular short story in China. Thereafter he wielded fiction and the essay as weapons, dissecting the old ritual order and the "bad roots of the national character" all his life.
luxun.ideas:
鲁迅一生的问题，不是书斋里的玄思，而是一声泣血的追问：这个古老的民族病在哪里，怎样才能活过来？
他给出的第一刀，砍向旧礼教。在《狂人日记》里，他借一个「狂人」的眼睛，翻开写满「仁义道德」的历史书，从字缝里只看出两个字——「吃人」。他的意思不是字面上的食人，而是说：那套以三纲五常、尊卑名分维系的旧秩序，在「天经地义」的名义下，无声地碾碎了无数人的生命与人格——被礼教逼死的寡妇、被科举废掉的读书人、被「孝」绑住的子女。讲和谐、讲安分、讲忍让，对踩在底层的人往往是镣铐。
他的第二刀，砍向「国民性」——一个民族在长期专制与苦难中养成的精神痼疾。他笔下的阿Q是最不朽的形象：受尽欺凌却从不正视失败，反而用「精神胜利法」自我安慰——被打了就想「儿子打老子」，于是心满意足。鲁迅借此照出一种普遍的国民心理：以自欺代替自省，以麻木代替反抗。他对同胞的态度，他自己概括为「哀其不幸，怒其不争」——既心疼他们的苦难，又愤恨他们的不觉醒。
但鲁迅决不是个简单的「全盘西化」论者，也不是守旧的「国粹」派。面对如何对待外来文化（与自家传统），他提出了著名的「拿来主义」：不必跪拜、也不必排斥，要像主人一样大胆地「拿来」——有用的拿来用，腐朽的烧掉，分清精华与糟粕，为我所用。这是一种清醒而不卑不亢的姿态。
他思想的底色，是「立人」：他相信，一个民族的根本出路，不在器物、不在制度的表面，而在唤醒一个个独立、清醒、有尊严的「人」。所以他弃医从文——医术只能治身体，文学才能治那沉睡麻木的灵魂。他的文字冷峻、犀利、悲愤，像一把解剖刀，却始终蘸着对这片土地最深的爱。他留下一句最沉的呼喊：「救救孩子……」
luxun.ideas_en:
Lu Xun's lifelong question was no study-bound speculation but a blood-wrung cry: where is the sickness of this ancient nation, and how can it be brought back to life?
His first cut struck the old ritual order. In "A Madman's Diary" he looked, through a "madman's" eyes, into a history book covered with the words "benevolence and righteousness," and saw between the lines only two characters—"eat people." He did not mean literal cannibalism, but that the old order held together by rigid hierarchy and the bonds of rank silently crushed countless lives and selves in the name of what was "natural and proper"—the widow driven to death by chastity codes, the scholar ruined by the examinations, the child shackled by "filial piety." Talk of harmony, of knowing one's place, of forbearance is often a fetter on those trampled at the bottom.
His second cut struck "national character"—the spiritual chronic disease a people grows in long ages of despotism and suffering. His Ah Q is the most immortal figure: endlessly bullied yet never facing his own defeat, consoling himself with the "method of spiritual victory"—beaten, he thinks "it's as if a son hit his father," and feels satisfied. Through him Lu Xun exposed a widespread psychology: self-deception in place of self-examination, numbness in place of resistance. His own attitude toward his people he summed up as "pity for their misfortune, anger at their failure to fight"—aching for their suffering, furious at their refusal to wake.
Yet Lu Xun was no simple "total Westernizer," nor a conservative "national essence" man. On how to treat foreign culture (and one's own tradition) he offered his famous "grabism" (nalai zhuyi): neither kneel before it nor reject it, but boldly "grab it" like a master of the house—take what is useful, burn what is rotten, tell the essence from the dross, and put it to your own use. It is a clear-eyed posture, neither servile nor arrogant.
The ground tone of his thought was "establishing the person": he believed a nation's real way out lies not in machines, nor on the surface of institutions, but in awakening one independent, clear-eyed, dignified "person" after another. That is why he left medicine for literature—medicine can heal only the body, while literature can heal the sleeping, numbed soul. His prose is cold, sharp, and grief-stricken, like a scalpel, yet always dipped in the deepest love for this land. He left one of the heaviest cries of all: "Save the children..."

assessments.text: 在《新民主主义论》中称鲁迅为「中国文化革命的主将」，是「伟大的文学家、思想家和革命家」，并称「鲁迅的骨头是最硬的」。这一定评也使鲁迅在后世被高度政治化地解读。
日本学者竹内好以《鲁迅》一书，把他读作一种「东方式现代性」的化身——在抵抗与挣扎中、而非简单模仿西方中走向现代的精神典型（大意）。

assessments_en.text: In On New Democracy, Mao called Lu Xun "the chief commander of China's cultural revolution," a "great writer, thinker, and revolutionary," saying "Lu Xun's bones were the hardest of all"—a canonization that also led later generations to read him in heavily politicized ways.

The Japanese scholar Takeuchi Yoshimi, in his book Lu Xun, read him as the embodiment of an "Eastern modernity"—a spirit that becomes modern through resistance and struggle rather than mere imitation of the West (paraphrased).

quotes: 其实地上本没有路，走的人多了，也便成了路。（《故乡》）
横眉冷对千夫指，俯首甘为孺子牛。（《自嘲》）
我向来是不惮以最坏的恶意，来推测中国人的。（《记念刘和珍君》）
救救孩子……（《狂人日记》结尾）
quotes_en: There was in fact no road on the earth to begin with; where many people pass, a road comes into being. (from "My Old Home")
Fierce-browed, I coolly defy a thousand pointing fingers; head bowed, I gladly serve as an ox for the children. (from "In Mockery of Myself")
I have never been reluctant to assume the very worst about my fellow Chinese. (from "In Memory of Liu Hezhen")
Save the children... (the closing words of "A Madman's Diary")
works: 小说集《呐喊》《彷徨》《故事新编》
杂文集《坟》《热风》《华盖集》《且介亭杂文》等
学术著作《中国小说史略》
works_en: The story collections Call to Arms, Wandering, and Old Tales Retold
The memoir Dawn Blossoms Plucked at Dusk
Essay collections (The Grave, Hot Wind, and more)
The scholarly History of Chinese Fiction
luxun.lineage: 新文化运动与中国现代文学的开山人物，确立了现代白话小说与杂文两种文体的范式，深刻影响了整个 20 世纪中国文学与思想。他大量译介俄苏及东欧弱小民族文学；虽被奉为左翼文学旗手，却始终保持独立的批判锋芒。
luxun.lineage_en: A founding figure of the New Culture Movement and of modern Chinese literature, he set the paradigm for both the modern vernacular short story and the critical essay, profoundly shaping twentieth-century Chinese letters and thought. He translated much Russian, Soviet, and Eastern European "small-nation" literature; though honored as the banner-bearer of left-wing writing, he kept an independent critical edge to the end.
luxun.trivia: 「幻灯片事件」是他弃医从文的转折；与胞弟周作人晚年决裂、终生未再往来；逝世时上海万人送葬，灵柩上覆盖着写有「民族魂」三字的白旗。
luxun.trivia_en: The "lantern-slide incident" was the turning point that led him from medicine to literature; he broke irreparably with his younger brother Zhou Zuoren and never reconciled; at his death tens of thousands joined the funeral procession in Shanghai, his coffin draped with a white banner bearing three characters: "Soul of the Nation."

nisbett.bio: 1941–，美国社会心理学家、文化心理学家，密歇根大学教授。早年与李·罗斯合著《人与情境》，是社会认知与「基本归因错误」研究的代表人物。后转向文化对思维方式的影响，2003 年出版《思维的版图》，系统提出东西方在认知方式上的系统差异，开文化心理学认知比较一脉。他也长期研究智力的可塑性，反对智力天定论。
nisbett.bio_en: 1941–, American social and cultural psychologist, professor at the University of Michigan. With Lee Ross he co-authored The Person and the Situation, a landmark in social cognition and the study of the "fundamental attribution error." He later turned to culture's effect on thinking, and in 2003 published The Geography of Thought, systematically proposing systematic East-West differences in modes of cognition and opening a line of cross-cultural comparison in psychology. He has also long studied the malleability of intelligence, opposing the view that it is fixed at birth.
nisbett.ideas:
尼斯贝特做了一件别人多半只在扶手椅上空谈的事：他把「东方人和西方人想问题的方式不一样」这个大而化之的印象，搬进了心理学实验室，变成可以测量、可以重复的数据。
他的核心发现，是两种思维风格的对照。西方人（尤其受古希腊传统影响的欧美人）偏「分析型」思维：注意力聚焦在单个「物体」上，习惯把它从背景中抽离，归入清晰的类别，再用形式逻辑去推理——非黑即白、A 不能同时是非 A。东亚人则偏「整体型」思维：注意力铺在整个「场」和关系网上，看重情境、联系与变化，更能容忍表面的矛盾，倾向「两边都有道理」的辩证调和。
这些都不是玄谈，而是实验结论。给人看一段水下动画，美国人开口先讲那条最醒目的大鱼，日本人却先描述池塘、水草、背景——西方盯焦点，东方看全局。在归因实验里，西方人更容易把一个人的行为归于他的「性格」，东亚人更会考虑他所处的「情境」。让人给「牛、鸡、草」分组，西方人倾向把牛和鸡归一类（都是动物，按类别），东亚人更可能把牛和草归一类（牛吃草，按关系）。
这些差异从哪来？他追溯到生态与社会结构：古希腊多商贸、航海、城邦辩论，催生独立的个体与对峙式逻辑；古代中国精耕稻作、聚族而居，互相依赖，催生重和谐、重关系的整体思维。语言、教育、哲学传统又把它代代强化。
但他最关键、也最反本质主义的一点是：**这两种风格不是刻在基因里、不可更改的「东方脑」「西方脑」。**它们是习惯，是可被环境塑造的。实验显示，只要给人启动另一种文化线索（比如让华裔美国人先看中式或美式图像），他的思维风格当场就会偏移；在两种文化里长大的人，更能在两种模式间自如切换。这意味着：认知方式可以学习、可以拓宽。他另一条贯穿性的主张与此呼应——智力同样不是天生注定的，而是可以靠环境与努力显著提升。
nisbett.ideas_en:
Nisbett did what others mostly only theorize about from an armchair: he took the sweeping impression that "Easterners and Westerners think differently" into the psychology lab and turned it into measurable, repeatable data.
His central finding is a contrast between two thinking styles. Westerners (especially Europeans and Americans shaped by the ancient Greek tradition) lean "analytic": attention fixes on a single "object," which they habitually detach from its background, sort into clear categories, and reason about with formal logic—black or white, A cannot also be not-A. East Asians lean "holistic": attention spreads across the whole "field" and web of relations, prizing context, connection, and change, more tolerant of surface contradiction, inclined toward a dialectical "both sides have a point."
These are not idle claims but experimental results. Shown an underwater animation, Americans open by describing the single most salient big fish, while Japanese first describe the pond, the plants, the background—the West fixes on the focal object, the East takes in the whole scene. In attribution experiments, Westerners more readily explain a person's behavior by their "character," East Asians more by the "situation." Asked to group "cow, chicken, grass," Westerners tend to put cow and chicken together (both animals, by category), East Asians are likelier to pair cow and grass (the cow eats grass, by relationship).
Where do these differences come from? He traces them to ecology and social structure: ancient Greece, with its trade, seafaring, and civic debate, bred the independent individual and adversarial logic; ancient China, with intensive rice farming and clustered kin living in mutual dependence, bred a holistic mind that prized harmony and relationship. Language, education, and philosophical tradition then reinforced it across generations.
But his most crucial, most anti-essentialist point is this: **these two styles are not genetically engraved, unchangeable "Eastern brains" and "Western brains."** They are habits, shaped by environment. Experiments show that merely priming another cultural cue (showing a Chinese-American person Chinese versus American images first) shifts their thinking style on the spot; people raised in two cultures switch between the two modes more freely. This means cognitive style can be learned and widened. His other running claim echoes this: intelligence, too, is not fixed at birth but can be raised substantially through environment and effort.

assessments.text: 诺贝尔经济学奖得主、心理学家卡尼曼多次表示，尼斯贝特关于推理与情境的研究对自己影响深远（大意）。
他于 1991 年获美国心理学会「杰出科学贡献奖」，被视为社会心理学与文化心理学领域最具影响力的学者之一。

assessments_en.text: The Nobel-winning psychologist Daniel Kahneman has said more than once that Nisbett's work on reasoning and the situation deeply influenced his own (paraphrased).
He received the APA's Distinguished Scientific Contribution Award in 1991 and is regarded as one of the most influential scholars in social and cultural psychology.

quotes: 我们看待世界的方式并非给定的、普世的，而是被文化深深塑造的。（《思维的版图》主旨，大意）
西方人看到的是一个个物体，东方人看到的是关系与场。（概括其核心实验，大意）
智力不是命中注定的，它在很大程度上可以被环境与努力改变。（其智力可塑论的概括，大意）
quotes_en: The way we see the world is not given and universal but deeply shaped by culture. (the thesis of The Geography of Thought; paraphrased)
Westerners see objects; East Asians see relationships and fields. (a summary of his core experiments; paraphrased)
Intelligence is not destiny; to a large degree it can be changed by environment and effort. (a summary of his view on malleable intelligence; paraphrased)
works: 《智力及其培养》(Intelligence and How to Get It, 2009)
works_en: The Person and the Situation (with Lee Ross)
Intelligence and How to Get It (2009)
nisbett.lineage: 承社会心理学的「情境主义」传统（勒温、费斯廷格、李·罗斯），开启了对东西方认知差异的实证比较，与北山忍、黑兹尔·马库斯关于「文化与自我」的研究互相呼应，共同奠定了当代文化心理学。
nisbett.lineage_en: Heir to the "situationist" tradition in social psychology (Lewin, Festinger, Lee Ross), he launched the empirical comparison of East-West cognition, resonating with the "culture and self" research of Shinobu Kitayama and Hazel Markus to jointly ground contemporary cultural psychology.
nisbett.trivia: 他早年是坚定的「认知普遍论」者，相信人类思维方式本质相同；据他自述，是在与来自东亚的学生（如彭凯平）反复讨论后，才被说服转向文化差异研究（大意）——一个「被自己学生改变了立场」的故事。
nisbett.trivia_en: He was for years a committed "cognitive universalist," convinced that human thinking is essentially the same everywhere; by his own account it was repeated discussions with students from East Asia (such as Kaiping Peng) that persuaded him to turn to the study of cultural differences (paraphrased)—a story of a scholar whose own students changed his mind.

bourdieu.bio: 皮埃尔·布迪厄（Pierre Bourdieu，1930–2002），法国社会学家，二十世纪后半叶最有影响力的社会理论家之一。出身法国西南部贝亚恩一个偏远村庄的邮差家庭，靠奖学金一路考进巴黎高等师范学院，这段从乡下穷孩子到巴黎学术精英的经历，让他终身对『出身如何隐形地决定命运』格外敏感。早年在阿尔及利亚服兵役并做田野，转向社会学；后长期任教于法兰西公学院。代表作《区隔》《实践理论大纲》《国家精英》等，晚年也是积极介入公共议题、为弱势者发声的公共知识分子。
bourdieu.bio_en: Pierre Bourdieu (1930–2002) was a French sociologist and one of the most influential social theorists of the latter twentieth century. Born to a postman's family in a remote village of Béarn in southwestern France, he rose by scholarships all the way to the École normale supérieure in Paris; this path from a poor country boy to a Parisian academic elite left him lifelong sensitive to 'how origin invisibly decides fate.' After military service and fieldwork in Algeria he turned to sociology, and later taught for many years at the Collège de France. His major works include Distinction, Outline of a Theory of Practice, and The State Nobility; in his later years he was also a public intellectual who actively engaged public issues and spoke for the disadvantaged.
bourdieu.ideas:
布迪厄一生都在回答一个问题：为什么社会的不平等，能一代代稳稳地复制下去，却让身处其中的人觉得『这很正常、是我自己的选择』？他给出的工具，是三个互相咬合的概念。
第一个是『资本』。我们通常以为资本就是钱，但布迪厄说，权力还有别的形态：『文化资本』——你的学历、谈吐、品味、对『高雅』事物的熟悉，这些都是从小在家庭里熏出来的；『社会资本』——你认识谁、能动用哪些关系；以及『符号资本』——声望、头衔、被人公认的『有面子』。这些资本都能互相兑换，也都能换成实实在在的位置与机会。一个出身优渥的孩子，未必更聪明，却天然握着满手文化与社会资本。
第二个是『惯习』（habitus）。这是布迪厄最精妙的概念：你的成长环境，会在你身上沉淀成一整套几乎无意识的倾向——你的口音、坐姿、什么让你自在、什么让你局促、你觉得『像我这样的人』该不该去争某个位置。它不是写下来的规则，而是长进身体里的本能。妙就妙在：惯习让被结构塑造的人，自愿地做出再生产这个结构的选择——穷孩子『自己选择』了不报考名校，并不觉得是被排斥，而觉得『那不适合我』。
第三个是『场域』（field）。社会不是铁板一块，而是由许多相对独立的『场域』组成——学术场、艺术场、政治场、某家公司，各有自己的游戏规则和最值钱的那种资本。进入一个场域，就像进入一局你未必懂规则的牌局：握着对路的资本、又有相称惯习的人，玩得游刃有余；不对路的人，处处别扭。
把三者合起来，布迪厄撕开了『精英靠才能、靠努力上位』这层温情面纱：很多被说成『天赋』『品味』『情商』的东西，其实是阶级特权穿上了中立的外衣。他最锋利的洞见是——最高明的权力，是让自己显得根本不像权力，让不平等看起来像自然秩序。认出这层伪装，正是反抗的第一步。
bourdieu.ideas_en:
Bourdieu spent his life answering one question: why does social inequality reproduce itself so steadily, generation after generation, while making those caught in it feel 'this is normal — it was my own choice'? His tools are three interlocking concepts.
The first is 'capital.' We usually think capital means money, but Bourdieu says power takes other forms too: 'cultural capital' — your credentials, your speech, your taste, your ease with 'refined' things, all absorbed from childhood at home; 'social capital' — whom you know and which relationships you can mobilize; and 'symbolic capital' — prestige, titles, being recognized as someone who 'has standing.' These forms convert into one another and into real positions and opportunities. A child of privilege is not necessarily smarter, yet naturally holds a full hand of cultural and social capital.
The second is 'habitus.' This is Bourdieu's most subtle concept: the environment you grow up in settles into you as a whole set of nearly unconscious dispositions — your accent, your posture, what puts you at ease and what makes you awkward, your sense of whether 'someone like me' should reach for a certain position. It is not a written rule but an instinct grown into the body. The cunning of it: habitus leads people shaped by a structure to make, willingly, the very choices that reproduce it — the poor child 'chooses for himself' not to apply to the elite school, feeling not excluded but that 'it isn't for me.'
The third is 'field.' Society is not one solid block but many relatively independent 'fields' — the academic field, the artistic field, the political field, a particular company — each with its own rules of the game and its own most valuable kind of capital. Entering a field is like joining a card game whose rules you may not know: those holding the right capital with a matching habitus play with ease; those out of sync are awkward at every turn.
Put together, these tear away the tender veil of 'elites rise by talent and effort': much of what gets called 'gift,' 'taste,' or 'emotional intelligence' is in fact class privilege dressed in neutral clothes. His sharpest insight: the subtlest power is the one that makes itself look like no power at all, that makes inequality look like the natural order. To see through this disguise is the first step of resistance.

assessments.text: 被广泛视为二十世纪最重要的社会学家之一；其『资本—惯习—场域』框架成为社会学、教育学、文化研究的基础工具，谷歌学术引用量长期位居社会科学前列。
常被批评理论过于强调结构再生产，对个体能动性与社会变迁的解释偏弱，文风晦涩冗长；也有人质疑其概念有时近乎不可证伪。

assessments_en.text: Widely regarded as one of the most important sociologists of the twentieth century; his 'capital–habitus–field' framework became a basic tool across sociology, education, and cultural studies, with citation counts long among the highest in the social sciences.

Often charged with over-emphasizing structural reproduction and underexplaining individual agency and social change, and with a dense, ponderous style; some question whether his concepts at times verge on the unfalsifiable.

quotes: 最成功的意识形态宣传，是用沉默实现的。（《实践理论大纲》大意）
品味分类着人，而分类者本身也被其分类所分类。（《区隔》大意）
社会学是一门搏击的科学。（访谈中常被引用的说法，大意）
quotes_en: The most successful ideological effects are those that have no need of words, but ask only a complicit silence. (paraphrased, Outline of a Theory of Practice)
Taste classifies, and it classifies the classifier. (paraphrased, Distinction)
Sociology is a martial art. (a remark often cited from interviews; paraphrased)
works_en: Distinction: A Social Critique of the Judgement of Taste (1979)
Outline of a Theory of Practice (1972)
bourdieu.lineage: 思想上承马克思（资本与阶级）、韦伯（地位与正当性）、涂尔干（社会事实），并与结构主义对话又超越之；影响遍及教育社会学、文化研究、人类学，学生与追随者众，晚年的公共介入也启发了后来的批判社会学。
bourdieu.lineage_en: Intellectually he drew on Marx (capital and class), Weber (status and legitimacy), and Durkheim (social facts), in dialogue with structuralism while moving beyond it; his influence spans the sociology of education, cultural studies, and anthropology, with many students and followers, and his late public engagement inspired later critical sociology.
bourdieu.trivia: 他出身贫寒，靠教育跻身法国学术顶层，却用一生的研究去揭穿『教育是公平阶梯』的神话——这份自我审视的张力贯穿其学术生涯。1995 年法国大罢工期间他公开站到罢工工人一边，成为媒体上著名的『介入型知识分子』。
bourdieu.trivia_en: Born poor, he rose through education into the summit of French academia, yet spent his life's research debunking the myth that 'education is a fair ladder' — a tension of self-scrutiny running through his career. During the 1995 French strikes he publicly took the side of the striking workers, becoming a famous 'engaged intellectual' in the media.

goffman.bio: 欧文·戈夫曼（Erving Goffman，1922–1982），加拿大裔美国社会学家，二十世纪最具原创性的微观社会学家之一。生于加拿大阿尔伯塔一个乌克兰犹太移民家庭，在芝加哥大学受训，受符号互动论传统影响。他擅长从最不起眼的日常细节——一次寒暄、一个眼神回避、医院里病人的处境——提炼出社会秩序的隐秘规则。曾任美国社会学协会主席，代表作《日常生活中的自我呈现》《污名》《精神病院》等，文风机智、冷峻，观察细致入微。
goffman.bio_en: Erving Goffman (1922–1982) was a Canadian-American sociologist and one of the most original micro-sociologists of the twentieth century. Born to a Ukrainian-Jewish immigrant family in Alberta, Canada, he was trained at the University of Chicago in the symbolic-interactionist tradition. He had a gift for distilling the hidden rules of social order from the most unremarkable everyday details — a greeting, an averted glance, the predicament of a patient in a hospital. He served as president of the American Sociological Association; his major works include The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life, Stigma, and Asylums, written in a witty, cool, finely observant style.
goffman.ideas:
戈夫曼最有名的洞见，是把社会生活看成一场永不落幕的戏剧——这就是『拟剧论』（dramaturgy）。他说，人与人相处时，每个人其实都在『表演』一个自我：我们挑选措辞、调整表情、管理姿态，向对方投射出一个希望被如此看待的形象。这不是说人虚伪，而是说『呈现自我』本就是社会互动的基本机制——你无法不表演。
他借舞台的比喻给出一对关键概念：『前台』与『后台』。前台，是你面对『观众』、按角色规范演出的场合——开会、见客户、站柜台时那个得体、专业、一切尽在掌握的你；后台，则是你卸下这套表演、可以松弛或排练的地方——后厨、休息室、和老友的私聊。前台维持形象，后台恢复元气；一个人若长期无处可退、永远在前台，会被掏空。
戈夫曼把这套表演的维护称作『印象管理』。我们时刻在不动声色地经营别人对自己的印象，而且这往往是合作性的：当有人当众出丑，旁人常会假装没看见，帮他把场子圆回来——他称之为维护共同的『情境定义』。社会秩序，很大程度上就靠这种心照不宣的、互相补台的微小默契撑着。
他另一个重要主题是『污名』（stigma）：当一个人身上带着某种被社会贬抑的标记（残疾、疾病、某种身份），他要如何管理这份『受损的身份』——是隐藏、是坦露，还是在能『过关』和暴露之间小心权衡。在《精神病院》里，他又走进精神病院这样的『全控机构』，揭示机构如何系统地剥夺一个人原有的自我。
戈夫曼的深刻在于：他证明了那些我们觉得最自然、最私人的东西——做自己、给人留个好印象、维持体面——其实都遵循着精密的社会脚本。读他，你会对人际互动多一层清醒，却不必因此变得犬儒：看穿表演，不等于否定真诚，而是更懂得人是如何在彼此面前小心地、也常是善意地，把生活演成可过下去的样子。
goffman.ideas_en:
Goffman's most famous insight is to see social life as a never-ending theatre — this is 'dramaturgy.' He says that when people are together, each is in fact 'performing' a self: we choose our words, adjust our expressions, manage our posture, projecting onto others an image we wish to be seen as. This does not mean people are fake; it means that 'presenting a self' is simply the basic mechanism of social interaction — you cannot not perform.
Using the stage metaphor he gives a key pair of concepts: 'front stage' and 'back stage.' The front stage is where you perform for an 'audience' according to a role's norms — the proper, professional, in-control you at a meeting, before a client, behind a counter; the back stage is where you drop that performance and can relax or rehearse — the kitchen, the staff room, a private chat with an old friend. The front stage maintains the image, the back stage restores energy; a person with nowhere to retreat, forever front-stage, is hollowed out.
Goffman calls the upkeep of this performance 'impression management.' We are constantly, unobtrusively, working on others' impressions of us, and this is often cooperative: when someone blunders in public, bystanders will often pretend not to notice and help them save face — he calls it preserving a shared 'definition of the situation.' Social order rests, to a great extent, on these tacit, mutually face-saving micro-courtesies.
Another of his major themes is 'stigma': when a person bears a socially devalued mark (a disability, an illness, a certain identity), how do they manage this 'spoiled identity' — to hide it, to disclose it, or to weigh carefully between 'passing' and exposure. In Asylums he enters the 'total institution' of the mental hospital, revealing how institutions systematically strip a person of their prior self.
Goffman's depth is this: he showed that the things we feel are most natural and most private — being ourselves, making a good impression, keeping our dignity — all follow precise social scripts. Reading him adds a layer of clarity to human interaction without making you cynical: to see through the performance is not to deny sincerity, but to understand better how people, carefully and often kindly, perform life before one another into something livable.

assessments.text: 被誉为二十世纪最具影响力的社会学家之一，开创了对面对面互动的系统研究，其概念（前台/后台、印象管理、污名、全控机构）已进入日常语言与多个学科。
有人批评其方法偏重敏锐观察而缺乏严格的可重复程序，理论碎片化、难以系统化；也有人认为他对结构性权力着墨不足。

assessments_en.text: Hailed as one of the most influential sociologists of the twentieth century, he pioneered the systematic study of face-to-face interaction, and his concepts (front/back stage, impression management, stigma, total institution) have entered everyday language and many disciplines.

Some fault his method as leaning on acute observation without rigorous, repeatable procedure, and as fragmentary and hard to systematize; others find that he gives too little weight to structural power.

quotes: 我们都在演戏，而且大多数时候，我们也相信自己所演的角色。（《日常生活中的自我呈现》大意）
世界确实是一场婚礼。（《日常生活中的自我呈现》语）
污名，是一种深深贬抑人的属性。（《污名》大意）
quotes_en: We are all just acting — and most of the time we also believe in the part we play. (paraphrased, The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life)
The world, in truth, is a wedding. (The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life)
Stigma is an attribute that is deeply discrediting. (paraphrased, Stigma)
works_en: The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life (1956)
Stigma: Notes on the Management of Spoiled Identity (1963)
goffman.lineage: 承芝加哥学派与符号互动论（米德、布鲁默）的传统，又自成一格；其拟剧论影响了社会学、社会心理学、传播学与表演研究，并预示了后来对身份、表演与日常生活的诸多探讨。
goffman.lineage_en: He carried on the Chicago School and symbolic-interactionist tradition (Mead, Blumer) while forging his own approach; his dramaturgy shaped sociology, social psychology, communication, and performance studies, foreshadowing much later inquiry into identity, performance, and everyday life.
goffman.trivia: 据说他常以近乎人类学家的姿态潜入各种场所做田野——为研究精神病院，他曾以体育馆助理的身份在一家医院待了近一年，从内部观察机构如何运作。他言辞犀利、不留情面的风格在学界亦有名。
goffman.trivia_en: He is said to have slipped into all sorts of settings to do fieldwork almost like an anthropologist — to study the mental hospital, he spent nearly a year in one posing as an assistant to the athletic director, observing from the inside how the institution worked. His sharp, unsparing manner was also well known in the academy.

hobbes.bio: 托马斯·霍布斯（Thomas Hobbes，1588–1679），英国哲学家，近代政治哲学的奠基者之一。生于英格兰，据其自述因西班牙无敌舰队来袭的恐慌而早产，他戏称自己『与恐惧是孪生兄弟』——这句玩笑也点中了他一生思想的底色。他博学多才，做过贵族家庭的家庭教师，游历欧洲，结识伽利略等人，并把几何学的演绎方法引入政治思考。英国内战的动荡是他思想的现实背景。代表作《利维坦》（1651）是政治哲学史上最重要的著作之一。
hobbes.bio_en: Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679) was an English philosopher and one of the founders of modern political philosophy. Born in England, by his own account prematurely amid the panic of the approaching Spanish Armada, he joked that he was 'twin-born with fear' — a quip that also names the keynote of his lifelong thought. Learned and versatile, he worked as a tutor to noble families, traveled Europe, met Galileo and others, and brought the deductive method of geometry into political thinking. The upheaval of the English Civil War was the real-world backdrop of his thought. His masterpiece, Leviathan (1651), is one of the most important works in the history of political philosophy.
hobbes.ideas:
霍布斯想解决一个被战乱逼到眼前的问题：人凭什么要服从一个政府？为什么需要权威？他的回答从一个著名的思想实验开始——设想没有任何政府、法律、警察的『自然状态』。
在自然状态里，人大体平等（再强的人，睡着时也可能被弱者杀死），都想自保、都追逐有限的资源，又彼此不信任。霍布斯冷峻地推断：这必然导致『一切人对一切人的战争』。注意，他不是说人天生邪恶，而是说在没有共同权威、人人自危的处境下，先下手、争抢、结盟自保，都是理性的。结果是他那句名言：这种生活『孤独、贫困、龌龊、野蛮而短暂』。在这里没有产业、没有文明，因为没人能指望安全地享有劳动成果。
出路是什么？人会出于对死亡的恐惧和对体面生活的渴望，运用理性达成一份『社会契约』：大家彼此约定，把各自动用暴力的权利让渡给一个共同的主权者，由它来制定并强制执行规则。这个主权者，他用《圣经》里的海怪命名为『利维坦』——一个由众人意志凝成的、令人敬畏的庞然权威。它之所以必要，是因为『没有刀剑约束的契约不过是一纸空文』：人们只有在确信别人也会守约（否则会被惩罚）时，才敢自己守约。
霍布斯的逻辑里藏着几个影响深远的洞见。其一，正当的权威不来自神授或传统，而来自人们为自保而达成的同意——这把政治的根基从天上拉回了人间，是社会契约论的开端。其二，秩序本身就是一种巨大的善：在他看来，再不完美的稳定秩序，也好过陷入无序的战争，因为无序会摧毁一切其他价值赖以存在的安全。这让他常被批评为替专制辩护；但更同情的读法是，他敏锐地指出了一个常被低估的真理——权力的真空从不会空着，你若不用规则去填，就会被混乱与强者的任意去填。理解了这一点，才谈得上如何把权威关进规则的笼子。
hobbes.ideas_en:
Hobbes set out to solve a problem the wars had pushed right up to his face: why should anyone obey a government? Why is authority needed at all? His answer begins with a famous thought experiment — imagine a 'state of nature' with no government, no law, no police.
In the state of nature people are roughly equal (even the strongest can be killed in his sleep by the weak), each wants self-preservation, each pursues scarce resources, and none trusts the others. Hobbes coldly deduces that this must lead to a 'war of all against all.' Note that he does not say people are innately evil, but that in a condition of no common authority where each fears all, striking first, grabbing, and forming protective alliances are all rational. The result is his famous line: such a life is 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.' Here there is no industry and no civilization, because no one can count on safely enjoying the fruits of his labor.
What is the way out? Out of fear of death and a desire for a decent life, people use reason to reach a 'social contract': all covenant with one another to surrender their right to use violence to a common sovereign, who makes and enforces the rules. This sovereign he names, after the biblical sea-monster, 'Leviathan' — an awe-inspiring colossus of authority congealed from the wills of the many. It is necessary because 'covenants without the sword are but words': people dare to keep their word only when assured that others will keep theirs too (on pain of punishment).
Hidden in Hobbes's logic are several far-reaching insights. First, legitimate authority comes not from divine right or tradition but from the consent people reach for self-preservation — this pulls the foundation of politics down from heaven to earth, and begins social-contract theory. Second, order itself is an immense good: in his view even an imperfect stable order is better than a descent into the war of disorder, because disorder destroys the very security on which all other values depend. This has often earned him the charge of apologizing for despotism; but a more sympathetic reading is that he sharply named an underrated truth — a power vacuum is never empty; if you do not fill it with rules, it will be filled by chaos and the arbitrary will of the strong. Only once this is understood can one even begin to ask how to cage authority within rules.

assessments.text: 公认为近代政治哲学与社会契约论的奠基者之一，《利维坦》对洛克、卢梭乃至整个自由主义传统都构成了必须回应的起点。
洛克、卢梭等后继者批评他赋予主权者的权力过大、近乎为绝对君权辩护；也有人质疑其对人性的描绘过于悲观、把竞争性的『自然状态』当成了普遍人性。

assessments_en.text: Recognized as a founder of modern political philosophy and social-contract theory; Leviathan became a starting point that Locke, Rousseau, and the whole liberal tradition had to answer.

Successors such as Locke and Rousseau charged him with granting the sovereign too much power, verging on a defense of absolute monarchy; others question whether his picture of human nature is too bleak, mistaking a competitive 'state of nature' for universal human nature.

quotes: （自然状态下的人生）孤独、贫困、龌龊、野蛮而短暂。（《利维坦》）
没有刀剑约束的契约不过是一纸空文。（《利维坦》大意）
人对人是狼。（拉丁谚语，霍布斯常被与之相联）
quotes_en: (The life of man in the state of nature is) solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short. (Leviathan)
Covenants, without the sword, are but words. (paraphrased, Leviathan)
Man is a wolf to man. (a Latin proverb often associated with Hobbes)
hobbes.lineage: 受伽利略与欧几里得的方法启发，把几何式演绎引入政治哲学；开社会契约论之先河，洛克、卢梭、康德皆在与他的对话中展开各自的政治理论，其影响延伸至现代政治学、博弈论与对国家正当性的讨论。
hobbes.lineage_en: Inspired by the methods of Galileo and Euclid, he brought geometric deduction into political philosophy; he pioneered social-contract theory, and Locke, Rousseau, and Kant each developed their political thought in dialogue with him, his influence reaching into modern political science, game theory, and debates over the legitimacy of the state.
hobbes.trivia: 他长寿而健康，相传八十多岁仍打网球，并在晚年翻译荷马史诗自娱。他与同时代的科学家、神学家论战不断，《利维坦》因其对教会权力的看法在当时备受争议，一度被指为异端。
hobbes.trivia_en: Long-lived and healthy, he is said to have still played tennis in his eighties and to have translated Homer for amusement in old age. He feuded endlessly with the scientists and theologians of his day, and Leviathan, for its views on church power, was highly controversial at the time and once branded heretical.

drucker.bio: 彼得·德鲁克（Peter Drucker，1909–2005），奥地利裔美国学者，被誉为『现代管理学之父』。生于维也纳一个文化氛围浓厚的家庭，少年时见证了奥匈帝国的崩解与两次大战间欧洲的动荡，这让他终身关注『一个能让人有尊严、有成就地工作的社会如何可能』。纳粹上台后他流亡英美，先做记者、经济学者，1940 年代受邀深入通用汽车考察，写成《公司的概念》，从此开创了把管理当作一门正经学问来研究的传统。著述近四十部，长期在大学执教与为企业、政府、非营利组织提供咨询。
drucker.bio_en: Peter Drucker (1909–2005) was an Austrian-American scholar hailed as the 'father of modern management.' Born in Vienna into a culturally rich household, in his youth he witnessed the collapse of the Austro-Hungarian Empire and the turmoil of interwar Europe, which left him lifelong concerned with 'how a society is possible in which people can work with dignity and achievement.' After the Nazis came to power he went into exile in Britain and America, working first as a journalist and economist; in the 1940s he was invited to study General Motors from within and wrote Concept of the Corporation, founding the tradition of treating management as a serious field of study. He wrote nearly forty books and long taught at universities while advising businesses, governments, and nonprofits.
drucker.ideas:
在德鲁克之前，『管理』几乎不被当成一门学问；他一生的工作，就是证明管理是一门关于『人』与『成果』的严肃实践，并且是现代社会最关键的器官之一。
他的起点是一个朴素却常被忘记的问题：一家企业到底是干什么的？流行的答案是『赚钱』，德鲁克说不对。利润是结果、是生存的条件，但企业存在的目的在它自身之外——是『创造顾客』。一个组织只有在外部世界（顾客、病人、读者）创造了真实价值，才有存在的理由。这一下子把人的注意力从内部的权力、流程、面子，扭向外部的成果。由此他反复强调一个区分：『效率』是把事情做对（do things right），『效果/效能』是做对的事情（do the right things）；先把方向搞对，远比把错的方向执行得再漂亮重要。
他最有名的工具是『目标管理』（MBO）：与其靠老板盯人、靠揣摩上意，不如让每个人都清楚自己要为整体贡献什么可检验的成果，并据此自我管理。它的精髓不是层层下压指标，而是让每个人都能把自己的工作，对准组织真正的目标——把『我很忙』『我很辛苦』替换成『我交付了什么』。
德鲁克还极早看见了时代的转向。1950 年代末，他就提出『知识工作者』的概念：现代经济越来越靠那些用知识与判断、而非体力创造价值的人，而这类人的产出很难像计件那样直接衡量，也无法靠监工式管理来驱动——你只能靠清晰的目标、信任与意义去引导。他由此预言了知识社会的到来。
贯穿这一切的，是一种近乎道德的底色。德鲁克坚持管理者首先要『做正确的事』，组织要承担社会责任，要让平凡的人做出不平凡的事、让人的长处发挥出来而非揪着短处不放。他常说自己其实是个『社会生态学家』，关心的从来不只是企业如何更赚钱，而是如何让组织成为一个能安顿现代人、给人尊严与归属的共同体。读德鲁克，最大的收获往往不是某个技巧，而是学会问对问题：我们到底想达成什么？我们正在用的衡量，是不是在奖励真正重要的东西？
drucker.ideas_en:
Before Drucker, 'management' was hardly treated as a discipline; his life's work was to show that management is a serious practice about 'people' and 'results,' and one of modern society's most crucial organs.
His starting point is a plain but often-forgotten question: what is a business actually for? The popular answer is 'to make money'; Drucker says no. Profit is a result and a condition of survival, but the purpose of a business lies outside itself — 'to create a customer.' An organization has a reason to exist only when it creates real value in the external world (customers, patients, readers). This at once turns attention away from internal power, process, and face, toward external results. From this he repeatedly stressed a distinction: 'efficiency' is doing things right, 'effectiveness' is doing the right things; getting the direction right matters far more than executing the wrong direction beautifully.
His most famous tool is 'management by objectives' (MBO): rather than have the boss police people and have people read the boss's mind, let everyone be clear about what verifiable result they must contribute to the whole, and manage themselves by it.
